where

η𝒊=(−1)𝒊x+𝒊y\eta_{\bm{i}}=(-1)^{{\bm{i}}_{x}+{\bm{i}}_{y}} (3.21)

identifies the checkerboard sublattices. Next, we insert these parameterizations into the spinon action, perform a gradient expansion, and transform the Lagrangian ℒJ{\cal L}_{J} into (aa is the lattice spacing)

ℒz\displaystyle{\cal L}_{z} =\displaystyle= ∫d2​r2​a2[ψ1​α∗(dd​τ+iaτ)ψ1​α+ψ2​α∗(dd​τ−iaτ)ψ2​α\displaystyle\int\frac{d^{2}r}{2a^{2}}\left[\psi_{1\alpha}^{\ast}\left(\frac{d}{d\tau}+ia_{\tau}\right)\psi_{1\alpha}+\psi_{2\alpha}^{\ast}\left(\frac{d}{d\tau}-ia_{\tau}\right)\psi_{2\alpha}\right. (3.22)
+λ¯​(|ψ1​α|2+|ψ2​α|2)−2​J​𝒬¯​(ψ1​α​ψ2​α+ψ1​α∗​ψ2​α∗)\displaystyle\qquad\qquad+\bar{\lambda}\left(|\psi_{1\alpha}|^{2}+|\psi_{2\alpha}|^{2}\right)-2J\bar{\mathcal{Q}}\left(\psi_{1\alpha}\psi_{2\alpha}+\psi_{1\alpha}^{\ast}\psi_{2\alpha}^{\ast}\right)
+(J/2)𝒬¯a2[(∇+i𝒂)ψ1​α(∇−i𝒂)ψ2​α\displaystyle\qquad\qquad+(J/2)\bar{\mathcal{Q}}a^{2}\left[\left({\bm{\nabla}}+i{\bm{a}}\right)\psi_{1\alpha}\left({\bm{\nabla}}-i{\bm{a}}\right)\psi_{2\alpha}\right.
+(∇−i𝒂)ψ1​α∗(∇+i𝒂)ψ2​α∗]].\displaystyle\qquad\qquad\qquad+\left.\left({\bm{\nabla}}-i{\bm{a}}\right)\psi_{1\alpha}^{\ast}\left({\bm{\nabla}}+i{\bm{a}}\right)\psi_{2\alpha}^{\ast}\right]\Biggr]\,.

We now introduce the fields

zα\displaystyle z_{\alpha} =\displaystyle= (ψ1​α+ψ2​α∗)/2\displaystyle(\psi_{1\alpha}+\psi_{2\alpha}^{\ast})/\sqrt{2}
πα\displaystyle\pi_{\alpha} =\displaystyle= (ψ1​α−ψ2​α∗)/2,\displaystyle(\psi_{1\alpha}-\psi_{2\alpha}^{\ast})/\sqrt{2}\,,

to map Eq. (3.22) to

ℒz\displaystyle{\cal L}_{z} =\displaystyle= ∫d2​r2​a2[πα∗(dd​τ+iaτ)zα−πα(dd​τ−iaτ)zα∗\displaystyle\int\frac{d^{2}r}{2a^{2}}\left[\pi_{\alpha}^{\ast}\left(\frac{d}{d\tau}+ia_{\tau}\right)z_{\alpha}-\pi_{\alpha}\left(\frac{d}{d\tau}-ia_{\tau}\right)z_{\alpha}^{\ast}\right. (3.23)
+λ¯​(|zα|2+|πα|2)−2​J​𝒬¯​(|zα|2−|πα|2)\displaystyle\qquad\qquad+\bar{\lambda}\left(|z_{\alpha}|^{2}+|\pi_{\alpha}|^{2}\right)-2J\bar{\mathcal{Q}}\left(|z_{\alpha}|^{2}-|\pi_{\alpha}|^{2}\right)
+(J/2)𝒬¯a2[|(∇+i𝒂)zα|2−|(∇+i𝒂)πα|2]].\displaystyle\qquad\qquad+(J/2)\bar{\mathcal{Q}}a^{2}\left[\left|\left({\bm{\nabla}}+i{\bm{a}}\right)z_{\alpha}\right|^{2}-\left|\left({\bm{\nabla}}+i{\bm{a}}\right)\pi_{\alpha}\right|^{2}\right]\Biggr]\,.

From Eq. (3.23), it is clear that the the π\pi fields have ‘mass’ λ¯+2​J​𝒬¯\bar{\lambda}+2J\bar{\mathcal{Q}}, while the zz fields have a mass λ¯−2​J​𝒬¯\bar{\lambda}-2J\bar{\mathcal{Q}} which vanishes at a quantum phase transition where the zαz_{\alpha} condense, leading to Néel order. The π\pi fields can therefore be safely integrated out, and ℒz{\cal L}_{z} yields the following effective action, valid at distances much larger than the lattice spacing [107, 108]:

Seff=∫d2​r4​2​a∫dτ{|(∂μ−iaμ)zα|2+Δ2c2|zα|2}.S_{\rm eff}=\int\frac{d^{2}r}{4\sqrt{2}a}\int d\tau\left\{|(\partial_{\mu}-ia_{\mu})z_{\alpha}|^{2}+\frac{\Delta^{2}}{c^{2}}|z^{\alpha}|^{2}\right\}\,. (3.24)

Here μ\mu extends over x,y,τx,y,\tau, c=2​J​𝒬¯​ac=\sqrt{2}J\bar{\mathcal{Q}}a is the spin-wave velocity, we have rescaled τ→τ/c\tau\rightarrow\tau/c, and Δ=(λ¯2−4​J2​𝒬¯12)1/2\Delta=(\bar{\lambda}^{2}-4J^{2}\bar{\mathcal{Q}}_{1}^{2})^{1/2} is the gap towards spinon excitations. Thus the long-wavelength theory describes a spin liquid with of a massive, spin-1/2, relativistic, boson zαz_{\alpha} (spinon) excitation coupled to a U(1) gauge field aμa_{\mu}.

The continuum theory also makes it easy to determine the fate of the antiferromagnet when the spin energy gap vanishes. We expect that zαz_{\alpha} will bose condense, and this will break the spin rotation symmetry; a term quartic in zαz_{\alpha} will be needed to stabilize the condensate. But zαz_{\alpha} carries a U(1) gauge charge, and so is not directly observable. Following the definitions of the underlying spin operators, it is not difficult to show that the gauge-invariant composite

𝓝=zα∗​𝝈α​β​zβ∼η𝒊​𝑺𝒊\bm{\mathcal{N}}=z_{\alpha}^{\ast}{\bm{\sigma}}_{\alpha\beta}z_{\beta}\sim\eta_{\bm{i}}{\bm{S}}_{\bm{i}} (3.25)

is just the Néel order parameter.

However, there is an important ingredient that our low energy theory has not yet considered. These are non-perturbative fluctuations of aμa_{\mu} which are Dirac monopoles in 2+1 dimensional spacetime. We will not carry out a full analysis here, and merely summarize some important consequences. An important result is that the spin liquid noted above is ultimately not a spin liquid. It is unstable to proliferation of monopoles, and ultimately confines a valence bond solid. But monopoles do not have a significant effect on the Néel state.

3.1.3 Quantum criticality

On general symmetry grounds, we extend Eq. (3.24) to a theory for the vicinity of the quantum critical point at which the spinon gap vanishes [223]:

𝒮U⁡(1)\displaystyle\mathcal{S}_{U(1)} =\displaystyle= ∫d3​x​(ℒz+ℒmonopole)+𝒮B\displaystyle\int d^{3}x\,\left(\mathcal{L}_{z}+\mathcal{L}_{\rm monopole}\right)+\mathcal{S}_{B}
ℒz\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{z} =\displaystyle= |(∂μ−iaμ)zα|2+g|zα|2+u(|zα|2)2+K(ϵμ​ν​λ∂νaλ)2\displaystyle|(\partial_{\mu}-ia_{\mu})z_{\alpha}|^{2}+g|z_{\alpha}|^{2}+u\left(|z_{\alpha}|^{2}\right)^{2}+K(\epsilon_{\mu\nu\lambda}\partial_{\nu}a_{\lambda})^{2}
ℒmonopole\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\rm monopole} =\displaystyle= −y⁡(ℳa+ℳa†)\displaystyle-y\left(\mathcal{M}_{a}+\mathcal{M}_{a}^{\dagger}\right)
𝒮B\displaystyle\mathcal{S}_{B} =\displaystyle= i​2​S​∑𝒊η𝒊​∫d​τ​a𝒊​τ.\displaystyle i2S\sum_{\bm{i}}\eta_{\bm{i}}\int d\tau\,a_{{\bm{i}}\tau}\,. (3.26)

The theory ℒz\mathcal{L}_{z} is also known as the ℂ​ℙ1\mathbb{CP}^{1} model. We have included monopoles ℳa\mathcal{M}_{a} in the gauge field aμa_{\mu}, and also the Berry phase of the spinons in the ground state.

As we tune the coupling gg in Eq. (3.26), we can expect the 2 phases shown in Fig. 14:
(i) Néel phase, g<gcg<g_{c}: the spinon zαz_{\alpha} condenses in a Higgs phase with ⟨zα⟩≠0\langle z_{\alpha}\rangle\neq 0. The aμa_{\mu} gauge field is Higgsed, and spin rotation symmetry is broken by opposite polarization of the spins on the two sublattices.
(ii) Valence bond solid (VBS), g>gcg>g_{c}: the spinons are gapped. For half-integer spin SS, there is broken translational symmetry by the crystallization of valence bonds in the pattern shown in Fig. 14.

We now obtain a potential gapless spin liquid if there is a continuous quantum phase transition at g=gcg=g_{c}. For half-integer spin SS, the single monopole terms in Eq. (3.26) average to zero at long wavelengths from the Berry phases, and only quadrupoled monopole terms survive. So we can simplify the continuum theory for the vicinity of the quantum critical point to [109, 110]

ℒz=|(∂μ−iaμ)zα|2+g|zα|2+u(|zα|2)2+K(ϵμ​ν​λ∂νaλ)2−y4(ℳa4+ℳa†4),\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\mathcal{L}_{z}=|(\partial_{\mu}-ia_{\mu})z_{\alpha}|^{2}+g|z_{\alpha}|^{2}+u\left(|z_{\alpha}|^{2}\right)^{2}+K(\epsilon_{\mu\nu\lambda}\partial_{\nu}a_{\lambda})^{2}-y_{4}\left(\mathcal{M}_{a}^{4}+\mathcal{M}_{a}^{\dagger 4}\right)\,, (3.27)

where y4y_{4} is the quadrupoled monopole fugacity. There is ample numerical evidence that y4y_{4} is irrelevant near a possible critical point, and so the question reduces to whether the theory ℒz\mathcal{L}_{z} at y4=0y_{4}=0 exhibits a critical point which realizes a conformal field theory in 2+1 dimensions. This is a question that has been studied extensively in numerics, and it is clear that a ‘deconfined critical’ description is suitable over a substantial length scale: with fractionalized spinons interacting with a U(1) gauge field in the absence of monopoles [115, 119, 120, 121, 122].

3.2 Fermionic partons

We now present an alternative analysis of the square lattice antiferromagnet in Eq. (3.1), replacing the bosonic partons in Eq. (3.5) by fermionic partons. This will ultimately lead to the same phase diagram as in Fig. 14, but with a dual description of the phases and the criticality. This dual fermionic description turns out to be the most efficient way to describe the connection between the critical spin liquid and dd-wave superconductivity in the doped antiferromagnet, as we will see in Section 4.

The following Schwinger fermion representation applies only for S=1/2S=1/2

𝑺𝒊=12​f𝒊​α†​𝝈α​β​f𝒊​β{\bm{S}}_{{\bm{i}}}=\frac{1}{2}f_{{\bm{i}}\alpha}^{\dagger}\,{\bm{\sigma}}_{\alpha\beta}\,f_{{\bm{i}}\beta} (3.28)

where f𝒊​αf_{{\bm{i}}\alpha} are canonical fermions obeying the constraint

∑αf𝒊​α†​f𝒊​α=1,for all 𝒊.\sum_{\alpha}f_{{\bm{i}}\alpha}^{\dagger}f_{{\bm{i}}\alpha}=1\quad,\quad\mbox{for all ${\bm{i}}$}. (3.29)

While the bosonic parton representation led to the U(1) gauge symmetry in Eq. (3.12), it turns out the Eqs. (3.28) and (3.29) have a larger SU(2) gauge invariance, and this will be crucial to our results. The analysis is clearest upon introducing a matrix notation for the fermions

ℱ𝒊≡(f𝒊↑−f𝒊↓f𝒊↓†f𝒊↑†)\mathcal{F}_{\bm{i}}\equiv\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}f_{{\bm{i}}\uparrow}&-f_{{\bm{i}}\downarrow}\\ f_{{\bm{i}}\downarrow}^{\dagger}&f_{{\bm{i}}\uparrow}^{\dagger}\end{array}\right) (3.30)

This matrix obeys the ‘reality’ condition

ℱ𝒊†=σy​ℱ𝒊T​σy.\mathcal{F}_{{\bm{i}}}^{\dagger}=\sigma^{y}\mathcal{F}_{{\bm{i}}}^{T}\sigma^{y}. (3.31)

Now we can write Eq. (3.28) as

𝑺𝒊=−14​Tr​(ℱ𝒊​σz​𝝈T​σz​ℱ𝒊†).{\bm{S}}_{{\bm{i}}}=-\frac{1}{4}\mbox{Tr}(\mathcal{F}_{{\bm{i}}}^{\phantom{\dagger}}\sigma^{z}{\bm{\sigma}}^{T}\sigma^{z}\mathcal{F}_{{\bm{i}}}^{\dagger})\,. (3.32)

The SU(2) gauge symmetry is now associated with a SU(2) matrix V𝒊V_{\bm{i}} under which [112, 113, 85]

ℱ𝒊→V𝒊​ℱ𝒊,\mathcal{F}_{\bm{i}}\rightarrow V_{\bm{i}}\,\mathcal{F}_{\bm{i}}\,, (3.33)

which is easily seen to leave the spin operator in Eq. (3.32) invariant. The global spin rotation symmetry is however

ℱ𝒊→ℱ𝒊​σz​RT​σz.\mathcal{F}_{\bm{i}}\rightarrow\mathcal{F}_{\bm{i}}\,\sigma^{z}R^{T}\sigma^{z}\,. (3.34)

where RR is the S=1/2S=1/2 spin rotation matrix defined by

(f𝒊↑f𝒊↓)→R​(f𝒊↑f𝒊↓).\left(\begin{array}[]{c}f_{{\bm{i}}\uparrow}\\ f_{{\bm{i}}\downarrow}\end{array}\right)\rightarrow R\left(\begin{array}[]{c}f_{{\bm{i}}\uparrow}\\ f_{{\bm{i}}\downarrow}\end{array}\right)\,. (3.35)

Next we insert Eq. (3.32) into Eq. (3.1), and perform Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation to obtain an effective Hamiltonian for the spinons, following the same procedure as for bosonic spinons. We skip the intermediate steps, and focus directly on the fermion bilinear Hamiltonian on symmetry grounds; we obtain the mean-field nearest-neighbor spin liquid Hamiltonian for the spinons of the π\pi-flux phase [111]:

ℋS​L​f\displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{SLf} =\displaystyle= i​J2​∑⟨𝒊​𝒋⟩e𝒊​𝒋​[Tr​(ℱ𝒊†​ℱ𝒋)−Tr​(ℱ𝒋†​ℱ𝒊)]\displaystyle\frac{iJ}{2}\sum_{\langle{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}\rangle}e_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}\left[\mbox{Tr}\left(\mathcal{F}_{{\bm{i}}}^{\dagger}\mathcal{F}_{{\bm{j}}}^{\phantom{\dagger}}\right)-\mbox{Tr}\left(\mathcal{F}_{{\bm{j}}}^{\dagger}\mathcal{F}_{{\bm{i}}}^{\phantom{\dagger}}\right)\right]
=\displaystyle= i​J​∑⟨𝒊​𝒋⟩e𝒊​𝒋​(Ψ𝒊†​Ψ𝒋−Ψ𝒋†​Ψ𝒊);Ψ𝒊≡(f𝒊↑f𝒊↓†),\displaystyle iJ\sum_{\langle{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}\rangle}e_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}\left(\Psi_{\bm{i}}^{\dagger}\Psi_{\bm{j}}-\Psi_{\bm{j}}^{\dagger}\Psi_{\bm{i}}\right);\quad\Psi_{\bm{i}}\equiv\left(\begin{array}[]{c}f_{{\bm{i}}\uparrow}\\ f_{{\bm{i}}\downarrow}^{\dagger}\end{array}\right),

where e𝒊​𝒋=±1e_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}=\pm 1 represents π\pi-flux on the fermions as shown in Fig. 15. We choose e𝒊​𝒋=−e𝒋​𝒊e_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}=-e_{{\bm{j}}{\bm{i}}} and

e𝒊,𝒊+𝒙^=1,e𝒊,𝒊+𝒚^=(−1)x,e_{{\bm{i}},{\bm{i}}+\hat{{\bm{x}}}}=1\,,\quad e_{{\bm{i}},{\bm{i}}+\hat{{\bm{y}}}}=(-1)^{x}\,, (3.39)

where 𝒊=(x,y){\bm{i}}=(x,y), 𝒙^=(1,0)\hat{\bm{x}}=(1,0), 𝒚^=(0,1)\hat{\bm{y}}=(0,1).

In the chosen form, it is evident that ℋS​l​f\mathcal{H}_{Slf} is invariant under the global spin rotation in Eq. (3.34), and also at least the gobal gauge transformation associate with Eq. (3.33). We have chosen the hopping to be pure imaginary because of the identity

Tr​(ℱ𝒊†​ℱ𝒋)=−Tr​(ℱ𝒋†​ℱ𝒊).\mbox{Tr}\left(\mathcal{F}_{{\bm{i}}}^{\dagger}\mathcal{F}_{{\bm{j}}}^{\phantom{\dagger}}\right)=-\mbox{Tr}\left(\mathcal{F}_{{\bm{j}}}^{\dagger}\mathcal{F}_{{\bm{i}}}^{\phantom{\dagger}}\right)\,. (3.40)

We can now easily diagonalize the Hamiltonion in Eq. (3.2), and obtain the fermionic dispersion spectrum analogous to Eq. (3.17)

ω𝒌=±2​J​(sin2⁡kx+sin2⁡ky)1/2.\omega_{\bm{k}}=\pm 2J\left(\sin^{2}k_{x}+\sin^{2}k_{y}\right)^{1/2}\,. (3.41)

We show a plot of this analogous to Fig. 13 in Fig. 16.

Unlike the bosonic spinons, the energy of the fermionic spinons is allowed to be negative, and the negative energy fermion states are occupied in the ground state. The constraint in Eq. (3.29) is then automatically satisfied. Notice the two independent nodal Dirac points at 𝒌v{\bm{k}}_{v}, v=1,2v=1,2 with

𝒌1=(0,0),𝒌2=(0,π).{\bm{k}}_{1}=(0,0)\quad,\quad{\bm{k}}_{2}=(0,\pi)\,. (3.42)

The index vv is the ‘valley’.

3.2.1 Low energy SU(2) gauge theory.

Going beyond mean field theory, while still remaining on the lattice, we extend the mean field Hamiltonian in Eq. (3.2) to be invariant under space-dependent SU(2) gauge symmetries. To achieve this, we need to introduce a SU(2) gauge field U𝒊​𝒋=U𝒋​𝒊†U_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}=U_{{\bm{j}}{\bm{i}}}^{\dagger} on each lattice link upon which the SU(2) gauge transformation acts as

U𝒊​𝒋→V𝒊​U𝒊​𝒋​V𝒋†.U_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}\rightarrow V_{\bm{i}}^{\phantom{\dagger}}U_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}V_{\bm{j}}^{\dagger}\,. (3.43)

Then, by gauge invariance, we extend Eq. (3.2) to

ℋS​L​f\displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{SLf} =\displaystyle= i​J2​∑⟨𝒊​𝒋⟩e𝒊​𝒋​[Tr​(ℱ𝒊†​U𝒊​𝒋​ℱ𝒋)−Tr​(ℱ𝒋†​U𝒋​𝒊​ℱ𝒊)]\displaystyle\frac{iJ}{2}\sum_{\langle{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}\rangle}e_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}\left[\mbox{Tr}\left(\mathcal{F}_{{\bm{i}}}^{\dagger}U_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}^{\phantom{\dagger}}\mathcal{F}_{{\bm{j}}}^{\phantom{\dagger}}\right)-\mbox{Tr}\left(\mathcal{F}_{{\bm{j}}}^{\dagger}U_{{\bm{j}}{\bm{i}}}^{\phantom{\dagger}}\mathcal{F}_{{\bm{i}}}^{\phantom{\dagger}}\right)\right]
=\displaystyle= i​J​∑⟨𝒊​𝒋⟩e𝒊​𝒋​(Ψ𝒊†​U𝒊​𝒋​Ψ𝒋−Ψ𝒋†​U𝒋​𝒊​Ψ𝒊);Ψ𝒊≡(f𝒊↑f𝒊↓†),\displaystyle iJ\sum_{\langle{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}\rangle}e_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}\left(\Psi_{\bm{i}}^{\dagger}U_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}^{\phantom{\dagger}}\Psi_{\bm{j}}-\Psi_{\bm{j}}^{\dagger}U_{{\bm{j}}{\bm{i}}}^{\phantom{\dagger}}\Psi_{\bm{i}}\right);\quad\Psi_{\bm{i}}\equiv\left(\begin{array}[]{c}f_{{\bm{i}}\uparrow}\\ f_{{\bm{i}}\downarrow}^{\dagger}\end{array}\right),

The first form in terms of ℱ\mathcal{F} makes both the SU(2) gauge invariance and the SU(2) spin rotation invariance explicit, while in the second form in terms of Ψ\Psi only the gauge invariance is explicit.

If we had not used the pure imaginary hopping in Eq. (3.2), then the mean-field Hamiltonian would break (‘Higgs’) the SU(2) gauge symmetry to a smaller symmetry. A ‘staggered flux’ ansatz which breaks the SU(2) down to U(1) has commonly been used in the literature [10]. However, it is now known that this U(1) spin liquid allows single monopole perturbations [224, 225] (unlike the quadrupole monopole perturbations in Eq. (3.27)), and such single monopole terms are expected to drive a strong instability to confinement. So we don’t consider the staggered-flux U(1) spin liquid.

The continuum formulation of this theory can be obtained by following the same procedure as in Section 3.1.2, but we have to carefully account for the SU(2) gauge symmetry. First, neglecting gauge fluctuations of U𝒊​𝒋U_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}} for now, let us write Eq. (3.2) in momentum space, in terms of the fermions ℱs​(𝒌)\mathcal{F}_{s}({\bm{k}}), where s=A,Bs=A,B is a sublattice index. Now the sublattices refer to sites with 𝒊x{\bm{i}}_{x} even and odd, which are the two sites in the unit cell. We obtain

ℋS​L​f=−J∑𝒌Tr(ℱ†(𝒌)[ρxsin(kx)+ρzsin(ky)]ℱ†(𝒌)),\displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{SLf}=-J\sum_{\bm{k}}\mbox{Tr}\left(\mathcal{F}^{\dagger}({\bm{k}})\left[\rho^{x}\sin(k_{x})+\rho^{z}\sin(k_{y})\right]\mathcal{F}^{\dagger}({\bm{k}})\right)\,, (3.47)

where ρℓ\rho^{\ell}, with ℓ=x,y,z\ell=x,y,z, are Pauli matrices in sublattice space. Next, analogous to Eq. (3.18), we take the continuum limit near the valley momenta in terms of 𝒳s​v​(𝒓,τ)\mathcal{X}_{sv}({\bm{r}},\tau)

ℱA​𝒊\displaystyle\mathcal{F}_{A{\bm{i}}} =\displaystyle= ∑v𝒳A​v​(𝒓,τ)​ei​𝒌v⋅𝒓i\displaystyle\sum_{v}\mathcal{X}_{Av}({\bm{r}},\tau)e^{i{\bm{k}}_{v}\cdot{\bm{r}}_{i}}
ℱB​𝒊\displaystyle\mathcal{F}_{B{\bm{i}}} =\displaystyle= ∑v𝒳B​v​(𝒓,τ)​ei​𝒌v⋅𝒓i\displaystyle\sum_{v}\mathcal{X}_{Bv}({\bm{r}},\tau)e^{i{\bm{k}}_{v}\cdot{\bm{r}}_{i}} (3.48)

for 𝒊{\bm{i}} on the A and B sublattices respectively. This yields the imaginary time Lagrangian density

ℒ𝒳=12Tr(𝒳†[∂τ+2Jiρx∂x+2Jiρzμz∂y]𝒳),\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{X}}=\frac{1}{2}\mbox{Tr}\left(\mathcal{X}^{\dagger}\left[\partial_{\tau}+2Ji\rho^{x}\partial_{x}+2Ji\rho^{z}\mu^{z}\partial_{y}\right]\mathcal{X}\right)\,, (3.49)

where μℓ\mu^{\ell} are the Pauli matrices in valley space. We recall that the fermion 𝒳s​v\mathcal{X}_{sv} has four-components, and each component is a 2×22\times 2 matrix which obeys the reality condition in Eq. (3.31). We can write this in a relativistic Dirac form

ℒ𝒳=i2​Tr​(𝒳¯​γμ​∂μ𝒳),\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{X}}=\frac{i}{2}\mbox{Tr}\left(\bar{\mathcal{X}}\gamma^{\mu}\partial_{\mu}\mathcal{X}\right)\,, (3.50)

with the definitions

𝒳¯=−i​𝒳†​γ0,γ0=ρy​μz,γx=ρz​μz,γy=−ρx,\bar{\mathcal{X}}=-i\mathcal{X}^{\dagger}\gamma^{0}\quad,\quad\gamma^{0}=\rho^{y}\mu^{z}\quad,\quad\gamma^{x}=\rho^{z}\mu^{z}\quad,\quad\gamma^{y}=-\rho^{x}\,, (3.51)

where we have absorbed factor of c=2​Jc=2J for the velocity of light. Finally, it is a simple matter to include the SU(2) gauge field by taking the continuum limit by writing

U𝒊​𝒋=exp⁡(−i​Ai​jℓ​σℓ)U_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}=\exp\left(-iA_{ij}^{\ell}\sigma^{\ell}\right) (3.52)

(where σℓ\sigma^{\ell} are the Pauli matrices in SU(2) gauge space) and expanding the exponential. We then obtain

ℒ𝒳=i2Tr(𝒳¯γμ[∂μ−iAμℓσℓ]𝒳).\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{X}}=\frac{i}{2}\mbox{Tr}\left(\bar{\mathcal{X}}\gamma^{\mu}\left[\partial_{\mu}-iA_{\mu}^{\ell}\sigma^{\ell}\right]\mathcal{X}\right)\,. (3.53)

The theory in Eq. (3.53) is the analog of the ℒz\mathcal{L}_{z} in Eq. (3.26) for bosonic spinons. The latter theory was a U(1) gauge theory with two relativistic complex scalars zαz_{\alpha}. In the present case, we have a SU(2) gauge theory with Nf=2N_{f}=2 massless Dirac fermions, associated with valley index vv. The global symmetry of zαz_{\alpha} was just spin rotations z→R​zz\rightarrow Rz. In contrast, here we have emergent global symmetry which combines spin and valley rotations. A first guess is a SU(4) symmetry generalizing Eq. (3.34)

𝒳→𝒳​L,\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{X}L\,, (3.54)

where LL acts on spin and valley space with L†​L=1L^{\dagger}L=1. However, imposition of the reality condition Eq. (3.31) shows that we also need

LT=σy​L†​σy,L^{T}=\sigma^{y}L^{\dagger}\sigma^{y}\,, (3.55)

and so the symmetry is only Sp(4)=SO(5)/ℤ2/\mathbb{Z}_{2} [226, 106]. In terms of the Hermitian Lie algebra elements MM, with L=ei​ML=e^{iM}, the reality condition is

MT=−σy​M​σy.M^{T}=-\sigma^{y}M\sigma^{y}\,. (3.56)

Requiring that MM commute with the γμ\gamma^{\mu}, we can now write down the 10 elements of the Lie algebra of Sp(4)=SO(5)/ℤ2/\mathbb{Z}_{2}

M={σx,σy,σz,μz​σx,μz​σy,μz​σz,ρx​μy,ρx​μx​σx,ρx​μx​σy,ρx​μx​σz}.M=\{\sigma^{x},\sigma^{y},\sigma^{z},\mu^{z}\sigma^{x},\mu^{z}\sigma^{y},\mu^{z}\sigma^{z},\rho^{x}\mu^{y},\rho^{x}\mu^{x}\sigma^{x},\rho^{x}\mu^{x}\sigma^{y},\rho^{x}\mu^{x}\sigma^{z}\}\,. (3.57)

The remaining 5 SU(4) generators which commute with the γμ\gamma^{\mu} are (t=1​…​5t=1\ldots 5)

Γt={μz,ρx​μx,ρx​μy​σx,ρx​μy​σy,ρx​μy​σz}.\Gamma^{t}=\{\mu^{z},\rho^{x}\mu^{x},\rho^{x}\mu^{y}\sigma^{x},\rho^{x}\mu^{y}\sigma^{y},\rho^{x}\mu^{y}\sigma^{z}\}\,. (3.58)

The Γt\Gamma^{t} all anti-commute with each other, and transform as a SO(5) vector under the generators in Eq. (3.57). It is now straightforward to check by working back to the lattice operators from the information above that the vector i​Tr​(𝒳¯​Γt​𝒳)i\mbox{Tr}\left(\bar{\mathcal{X}}\Gamma^{t}\mathcal{X}\right) corresponds precisely to the 5 components of the orders parameters shown in Fig. 14: the first two components are the VBS order, and the last 3 components are the Néel order 𝓝\bm{\mathcal{N}} in Eq. (3.25) [226, 106].

Wang et al. [106] have argued that the likely fate of the SU(2) gauge theory upon confinement is a state which the SO(5) symmetry is spontaneously broken with ⟨i​Tr​(𝒳¯​Γt​𝒳)⟩≠0\langle i\mbox{Tr}\left(\bar{\mathcal{X}}\Gamma^{t}\mathcal{X}\right)\rangle\neq 0. The lattice model does not have exact SO(5) symmetry, and the choice between the Néel and VBS components of Γt\Gamma^{t} is made by additional 4-fermi terms that can be added to Eq. (3.53). So the ultimate fate of the theory is essentially identical to the fate of the bosonic spinon theory in Section 3.1, as illustrated in Fig. 14. This is essentially the reason for the duality between the theories in Section 3.1.3 and 3.2.1, and Wang et al. have provided additional topological arguments.

3.3 SO(5) non-linear σ\sigma-model

There is a third formulation of the theories in Section 3.1.3 and 3.2.1 which is useful for some purposes, as we illustrate in Fig. 17.

This is obtained most simply by coupling Eq. (3.53) to the SO(5) vector order parameter, and integrating out the fermions. Introducing the SO(5) fundamental unit length field ntn_{t}, nt​nt=1n_{t}n_{t}=1 to Eq. (3.53)

ℒ𝒳​n=i2Tr(𝒳¯γμ[∂μ−iAμℓσℓ]𝒳)−intTr(𝒳¯Γt𝒳),\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{X}n}=\frac{i}{2}\mbox{Tr}\left(\bar{\mathcal{X}}\gamma^{\mu}\left[\partial_{\mu}-iA_{\mu}^{\ell}\sigma^{\ell}\right]\mathcal{X}\right)-in_{t}\mbox{Tr}\left(\bar{\mathcal{X}}\Gamma^{t}\mathcal{X}\right)\,, (3.59)

we integrate out the Dirac fermions following the analysis of Ref. [227] and obtain

ℒn=12​g​(∂μnt)2+2​π​i​Γ​[nt]\mathcal{L}_{n}=\frac{1}{2g}\left(\partial_{\mu}n_{t}\right)^{2}+2\pi i\Gamma[n_{t}] (3.60)

The last term is the Wess-Zumino-Witten (WZW) term at level 1: it is a Berry phase associated with spacetime textures of ntn_{t}, a higher dimensional analog of the Berry phase of a single spin which is proportional to area enclosed by a spherical path [228, 106]: an explicit expression of Γ⁡[nt]\Gamma[n_{t}] requires 4+1 dimensions with an emergent spatial direction. Upon reduction to a O(3) non-linear sigma model for the Néel order parameter 𝓝\bm{\mathcal{N}} in Eq. (3.25), the WZW term reduces [229] to the Berry phases of the monopoles noted near Eq. (3.27).

Also, note that while the SO(5) symmetry is explicit in the fermionic spinon theory in Eq. (3.53), it is not explicit in the bosonic spinon theory in Eq. (3.27), but expected to be emergent [230].

The form in Eq. (3.60) has been exploited in recent numerical work on the fuzzy sphere [118]. Their results, and those of a number of other numerical works [114, 115, 116, 117, 119, 120, 121, 122] show that the critical spin liquid defined by Eq. (3.27), Eq. (3.53), or (3.60) is stable over a substantial intermediate energy and length scales, before ultimately confining into a Néel or VBS state. This intermediate range stability is not a bug, but a feature ideal for our purposes of defining a FL* state at intermediate temperatures, which ultimately confines to variety of other states at low temperatures.

3.4 Direct observation of spinons

We now discuss possible experimental evidence for the spinons of the deconfined critical state of Fig. 17 in the cuprate compounds.

In the insulating antiferromagnet, higher energy neutron scattering has been interpreted using spinons by Headings et al. [123] and Dalla Piazza et al. [124].

For the doped system, it has recently been argued [135, 138] that RIXS measurements [231, 232] do indeed provide support for the presence of spinons. At half-filling, there is sharp spin wave excitation extending to high energy ∼400\sim 400meV. This excitation survives upon doping even at high energies, but becomes much broader. This broad spectrum has similarities to that expected from the π\pi-flux spin liquid, as computed near the destruction of the Néel order in the insulating J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} model by Ref. [233]. See Figs. 8 and 9 in Ref. [138] for a comparison. Ref. [234] has considered the influence of charge order on the fermionic spinons, and shown that it can reproduce the ‘hourglass’ structure of the incommensurate spin corrections.

Another issue in the comparison with the cuprates is that the free fermion theory of the π\pi-flux phase predicts a gapless spin spectrum near momenta (π,0)(\pi,0) and (0,π)(0,\pi), and low energy spin excitations have not been observed at these momenta. However, Ref. [135] has argued that this spectrum is suppressed by SU(2) gauge fluctuations. Their argument is based upon the scaling dimensions of the associated operators as measured by fuzzy-sphere analysis [118] of the SO(5) theory reviewed in Section 3.3.

In the following discussion of the doped system, we will see that the spinons fαf_{\alpha} in ℋS​L​f\mathcal{H}_{SLf} play a crucial role in the theory of the observed electronic spectrum in Sections 5.1, 6.1, and 6.3. We can interpret this successful description of the electronic spectrum as an indirect observation of spinons.

4 Confinement to dd-wave superconductivity and charge order at half-filling

We have so far considered the square lattice antiferromagnet as an insulator with an essentially infinite gap to electrically charged excitations. In the following discussion, we will build on the low energy theory of such an antiferromagnet as a SU(2) gauge theory coupled to fermionic spinons in Eq. (3.2.1). We have argued that the phase diagram of such a theory is as in Fig. 14 i.e. except possibly in a critical region, the SU(2) gauge theory confines at low energies, and we obtain either the Néel or VBS states.

We now wish to consider a more general situation in which the gap to charged excitations can vanish [235]. In the cuprates, gapless charged excitations appear when we dope the antiferromagnet. We will consider this important situation in the following sections. But for now we consider the simpler case where the charge gap vanishes while the electronic density remains the same as in an insulator. We emphasize that the present section describes such a charge gap vanishing transition without using the ALM, and using only symmetry arguments. We will resume explicit use of the ALM in Section 5 when we consider the doped case, although we can also proceed there with only symmetry arguments.

We work at half-filling and also assume particle-hole symmetry as it simplifies the analysis. We can decrease the charge gap by describing the insulator by an underlying Hubbard model with on-site repulsion UU, and reducing the value of UU, or by adding additional off-site interactions. Such models have been considered in numerical studies [236, 237, 238, 239, 240, 241, 242, 243, 244, 245, 246, 247]. We will now show that the SU(2) gauge theory of Eq. (3.2.1) has other possible fates once charged excitations are included, the most interesting of which is a dd-wave superconductor with gapless nodal quasiparticles.

In terms of adiabatic continuity, this dd-wave superconductor is precisely the superconductor observed in the cuprates. However, the dd-wave superconductor obtained in this section has one significant quantitative difference from the observations, noted in Section 1: it has a Lorentz-invariant form of its dispersion, with the two velocities only the square lattice diagonals, vFv_{F} and vΔv_{\Delta}, being equal to each other (see Fig. 26B). The cuprates instead have vF≫vΔv_{F}\gg v_{\Delta}. We will resolve this problem in an interesting manner in Section 6.1 when we consider the transition from FL* to a dd-wave superconductor in the doped case.

The only matter field in Section 3.2 is the fermion ℱ\mathcal{F}, which has electrical charge 0, spin 1/21/2, and is a gauge SU(2) fundamental. As we are allowing for charged fluctuations, we need to define an electron operator, which has charge −e-e, spin 1/21/2, and is a gauge SU(2) singlet. This directly leads us to introducing a boson BB which has charge +e+e, spin 0, and is a gauge SU(2) fundamental, so that a composite of ℱ\mathcal{F} and BB will have the same quantum numbers as the electron. We now show that this information is basically sufficient to deduce an effective action for BB, and to reach our main conclusions. We will give a more microscopic definition of the field BB in the doped case later near Eq. (5.3).

A boson with the same quantum numbers as our BB was introduced in earlier work [113, 85, 128, 248], but with an important difference. In the earlier work, the expectation value of B†​BB^{\dagger}B was set to be equal to the doping density. That is not the case in our work, as the doping density also includes the density of fermionic holes (see Section 2). In this section, we are considering the particle-hole symmetric case at half-filling, and ⟨B†​B⟩\langle B^{\dagger}B\rangle is non-zero even though there is no doping (this is similar to the situation in the superfluid-insulator transition of bosons [249]).

Similar to Eq. (3.30), we introduce a matrix notation for the electron 𝒞\mathcal{C} and the boson BB:

𝒞𝒊≡(c𝒊↑−c𝒊↓c𝒊↓†c𝒊↑†),B𝒊≡(B1​𝒊B2​𝒊),ℬ𝒊≡(B1​𝒊−B2​𝒊∗B2​𝒊B1​𝒊∗),\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{\bm{i}}\equiv\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}c_{{\bm{i}}\uparrow}&-c_{{\bm{i}}\downarrow}\\ c_{{\bm{i}}\downarrow}^{\dagger}&c_{{\bm{i}}\uparrow}^{\dagger}\end{array}\right)\,,\quad B_{\bm{i}}\equiv\left(\begin{array}[]{c}B_{1{\bm{i}}}\\ B_{2{\bm{i}}}\end{array}\right)\,,\quad\mathcal{B}_{\bm{i}}\equiv\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}B_{1{\bm{i}}}&-B_{2{\bm{i}}}^{\ast}\\ B_{2{\bm{i}}}&B_{1{\bm{i}}}^{\ast}\end{array}\right)\,,

By matching these gauge, spin rotation, and charge conservation symmetries we deduce that the operator correspondence between the electrons, the Higgs boson BB, and the fermionic spinons must be

𝒞𝒊∼ℬ𝒊†​ℱ𝒊.\mathcal{C}_{{\bm{i}}}^{\vphantom{\dagger}}\sim\mathcal{B}_{\bm{i}}^{\dagger}\,\mathcal{F}_{\bm{i}}^{\vphantom{\dagger}}\,. (4.14)

We now obtain an energy functional for BB in a Landau-type expansion [105]. Such a functional must also involve the gauge field U𝒊​𝒋U_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}} to maintain gauge invariance. The fermion ff experiences a π\pi flux with pure imaginary hopping, while the electron cc has purely real hopping with zero flux (in the absence of an applied physical magnetic field). From these facts and Eq. (4.14) we reach the important conclusion that the boson BB must also have purely imaginary hopping with π\pi-flux (the i​wiw term in Eq. (4.17) below). So the relation

Tx​Ty=−Ty​Tx,T_{x}T_{y}=-T_{y}T_{x}\,, (4.16)

realizing the π\pi-flux applies both to the spinons and to BB. We can also reach these conclusions, and obtain other constraints, by examining the action of all symmetry operators of ff, and use Eq. (4.14) to deduce the action of symmetry operations on BB: the results are summarized in Table 1.

(4.18)

These relations are the key to BB providing a fractionalized description of intertwined orders. We have retained terms involving nearest neighbor sites in Eq. (4.17), and a few terms with longer-range density-density interactions.

Fig. 18 shows a phase diagram obtained by minimizing the energy functional with nearest-neighbor interactions only (V11=V22=0V_{11}=V_{22}=0). Three phases are found, also illustrated in Fig. 18:

  1. A.

    This state A charge stripe order with period 2, centered on the sites.

  2. B.

    A dd-wave superconductor, with Δ𝒊,𝒊+𝒙^=−Δ𝒊,𝒊+𝒚^\Delta_{{\bm{i}},{\bm{i}}+\hat{\bm{x}}}=-\Delta_{{\bm{i}},{\bm{i}}+\hat{\bm{y}}}.

  3. C.

    A “dd-density wave” state which has a staggered pattern of spontaneous current.

An interesting feature is that these orders are degenerate in the quadratic energy functional ℰ2\mathcal{E}_{2}, and the degeneracy is broken only at quartic order in ℰ4\mathcal{E}_{4}. The fact that the leading term is degenerate provides a rationale for nearly-degenerate multiple competing or ‘intertwined’ orders [105]; more conventional Landau theory approaches [62, 63, 64, 65, 67, 66, 68, 69] do not have any term in which the degeneracy is exact without fine-tuning.

Our primary interest for now is phase B. Remarkably, the structure of the π\pi-flux spin liquid, and consequently the π\pi-flux on BB leads to dd-wave pairing, and not ss-wave pairing. Also, once BB is condensed, we can identify c∼fc\sim f via Eq. (4.14), and so the electron spectral function will inherit nodal Bogoliubov quasiparticles from the massless Dirac spinons. The main phenomenological difficulty, as noted earlier, is that the Bogoliubov quasiparticles will have isotropic dispersion, as in Eq. (3.41) and Fig. 16. However, other features of the dd-wave state obtained from the energy functional in Eq. (4.17) do match observations, including vortices with flux h/(2​e)h/(2e) (despite the boson BB having charge ee), and intertwined charge order halos of vortex cores. As these features apply also to the doped case, we defer their discussion to Section 6, where we will also fix the difficulty with the anisotropic velocities in Section 6.1.

We now discuss more global aspects of the phase diagram shown in Fig. 18, as a function of the tuning parameter rr, which is the ‘mass’ of BB.

  • •

    When rr is large and positive, then we can ignore the BB sector, and revert to the spinon only theory of Section 3.2. The low energy theory is Eq. (3.53), and we expect a confining insulator with either Néel or VBS order as the ground state.

  • •

    When rr is negative, BB condenses, and this has the salutary effect of making the gauge field AA massive, as in the Higgs phenomenon. In this case, a mean-field treatment of interactions in the bosonic sector only is qualitatively valid, and we obtain one of three states A,B,C listed above.

It is also interesting to consider the nature of the low energy theory when we approach the Higgs condensation transition [235]. The dispersion of the BB bosons is the same as that of the ff fermions, apart from an overall constant - see Fig. 19.

While the low energy fermions are at the Fermi level in the middle of the band, the low energy bosons will condense near the bottom of the band. Because there are two such minima in the π\pi-flux band structure, we can identify two valleys v=1^,2^v=\hat{1},\hat{2}, and introduce a continuum field B^a​v\hat{B}_{av} for the low energy theory, where a=1,2a=1,2 is a SU(2) gauge space index (this is similar to Section 3.1.2). From the lattice transformations in Table 1, we can also relate the order parameters A,B,C to gauge-invariant bilinears of B^\hat{B}

dd-wave superconductor :εa​b​B^a​1^​B^b​2^≡Δ\displaystyle:~~\varepsilon_{ab}\hat{B}_{a\hat{1}}\hat{B}_{b\hat{2}}\equiv\Delta
xx-CDW :B^a​1^∗​B^a​1^−B^a​2^∗​B^a​2^≡B^†​μz​B^\displaystyle:~~\hat{B}_{a\hat{1}}^{\ast}\hat{B}_{a\hat{1}}^{\phantom{\dagger}}-\hat{B}_{a\hat{2}}^{\ast}\hat{B}_{a\hat{2}}^{\phantom{\dagger}}\equiv\hat{B}^{\dagger}\mu^{z}\hat{B}^{\phantom{\dagger}}

Here μℓ\mu^{\ell} are the Pauli matrices acting in the boson valley space of Fig. 19.

We now assume that the quartic couplings of BB are such that the ground state in the Higgs phase is a dd-wave superconductor. Then, we can sketch the phase diagram in Fig. 20 with the 3 important phases - Néel, VBS, and dd-wave superconductivity. Near the onset of the BB condensate, we extend the spinon continuum theory of Eq. (3.53) to also include phases A,B,C by adding a continuum Lagrangian for B^\hat{B}:

ℒ𝒳​B^=ℒ𝒳+|(∂μ−iAμℓσℓ)B^|2+r|B^|2+u¯|B^|4\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{X}\hat{B}}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{X}}+\left|\left(\partial_{\mu}-iA_{\mu}^{\ell}\sigma^{\ell}\right)\hat{B}\right|^{2}+r|\hat{B}|^{2}+\bar{u}|\hat{B}|^{4}
+v1​(B^†​μz​B^)2+v1​(B^†​μx​B^)2+v2​(B^†​μy​B^)2+v3​|εa​b​B^a​1​B^b​2|2.\displaystyle+v_{1}\left(\hat{B}^{\dagger}\mu^{z}\hat{B}\right)^{2}+v_{1}\left(\hat{B}^{\dagger}\mu^{x}\hat{B}\right)^{2}+v_{2}\left(\hat{B}^{\dagger}\mu^{y}\hat{B}\right)^{2}+v_{3}\left|\varepsilon_{ab}\hat{B}_{a1}\hat{B}_{b2}\right|^{2}\,.
