5 SU(2) gauge theory of the cuprate pseudogap

Now we return to the analysis of the pseudogap using the ALM in Eq. (2.10). In Section 2.2.2, we presented a mean field analysis in terms of decoupled Kondo lattice and spin liquid models. This section will couple them using the methods developed in Sections 3 and 4.

On the spin liquid layer of 𝑺2{\bm{S}}_{2} spins we write a parton decomposition which parallels that in Eq. (3.28)

𝑺2​𝒊=12​f𝒊​α†​𝝈α​β​f𝒊​β.\displaystyle{\bm{S}}_{2{\bm{i}}}=\frac{1}{2}f_{{\bm{i}}\alpha}^{\dagger}{\bm{\sigma}}_{\alpha\beta}^{\vphantom{\dagger}}f_{{\bm{i}}\beta}^{\vphantom{\dagger}}\,. (5.1)

Then the analysis of the exchange interactions within the 𝑺2{\bm{S}}_{2} layer is precisely that in Section 3.2. W decouple the J𝒊​𝒋J_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}} term in Eq. (2.10) to ℋS​L​f\mathcal{H}_{SLf} in Eq. (3.2.1) realizing a π\pi-flux state of the 𝑺2{\bm{S}}_{2} spins with a SU(2) gauge field.

To couple this spin liquid to the Kondo lattice, we have to decouple the J⟂J_{\perp} term coupling the f1f_{1} and ff spinons. Given the SU(2) gauge structure of the 𝑺2{\bm{S}}_{2} layer, it pays to decouple the J⟂J_{\perp} term in a manner which keeps the SU(2) gauge invariance explicit. In fact, the needed decoupling field is precisely the boson ℬ𝒊\mathcal{B}_{\bm{i}} introduced in Eq. (4). We also introduce a matrix fermion operator ℱ1​𝒊\mathcal{F}_{1{\bm{i}}}

ℱ1​𝒊≡(f1​𝒊↑−f1​𝒊↓f1​𝒊↓†f1​𝒊↑†),\mathcal{F}_{1{\bm{i}}}\equiv\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}f_{1{\bm{i}}\uparrow}&-f_{1{\bm{i}}\downarrow}\\ f_{1{\bm{i}}\downarrow}^{\dagger}&f_{1{\bm{i}}\uparrow}^{\dagger}\end{array}\right), (5.2)

whose transformations under the symmetries in Eqs. (4.8,4.9,4.10) are the same as those of 𝒞𝒊\mathcal{C}_{\bm{i}}. We summarize the gauge and symmetry properties in Table 2.

Then, from the J⟂J_{\perp} term, symmetry considerations are sufficient to constrain the structure of the Yukawa term between B{B} and the fermions [105], which follows from Eq. (4.14) and is illustrated in Fig. 21:

ℋY\displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{Y} =−12∑𝒊[iTr(ℱ1​𝒊†ℬ𝒊†ℱi)+igTr(𝒞𝒊†ℬ𝒊†ℱi)+H.c.]\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\bm{i}}\left[i\,\mbox{Tr}\left(\mathcal{F}_{1{\bm{i}}}^{\dagger}\mathcal{B}_{{\bm{i}}}^{\dagger}\mathcal{F}_{i}^{\vphantom{\dagger}}\right)+ig\,\mbox{Tr}\left(\mathcal{C}_{{\bm{i}}}^{\dagger}\mathcal{B}_{{\bm{i}}}^{\dagger}\mathcal{F}_{i}^{\vphantom{\dagger}}\right)+\mbox{H.c.}\right] (5.3)
=∑𝒊[i(B1​𝒊f𝒊​α†f1​𝒊​α−B2​𝒊εα​βf𝒊​αf1​𝒊​β)+H.c.\displaystyle=\sum_{\bm{i}}\left[i\left(B_{1{\bm{i}}}^{\vphantom{\dagger}}f_{{\bm{i}}\alpha}^{\dagger}f_{1{\bm{i}}\alpha}^{\vphantom{\dagger}}-B_{2{\bm{i}}}^{\vphantom{\dagger}}\varepsilon_{\alpha\beta}^{\vphantom{\dagger}}f_{{\bm{i}}\alpha}^{\vphantom{\dagger}}f_{1{\bm{i}}\beta}^{\vphantom{\dagger}}\right)+\mbox{H.c.}\right.
+ig(B1​𝒊f𝒊​α†c𝒊​α−B2​𝒊εα​βf𝒊​αc𝒊​β)+H.c.],\displaystyle~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~\left.+ig\left(B_{1{\bm{i}}}^{\vphantom{\dagger}}f_{{\bm{i}}\alpha}^{\dagger}c_{{\bm{i}}\alpha}^{\vphantom{\dagger}}-B_{2{\bm{i}}}^{\vphantom{\dagger}}\varepsilon_{\alpha\beta}^{\vphantom{\dagger}}f_{{\bm{i}}\alpha}^{\vphantom{\dagger}}c_{{\bm{i}}\beta}^{\vphantom{\dagger}}\right)+\mbox{H.c.}\right]\,,

We have also included a Yukawa coupling to cαc_{\alpha} from an allowed term ∼𝑺2​𝒊⋅c𝒊​α†​𝝈α​β​c𝒊​β\sim{\bm{S}}_{2{\bm{i}}}\cdot c_{{\bm{i}}\alpha}^{\dagger}{\bm{\sigma}}_{\alpha\beta}c_{{\bm{i}}\beta}, which descends from the Kondo coupling noted below Eq. (2.9).

We can now collect all terms to write down the complete Hamiltonian needed for our analysis of the pseudogap metal, and its low temperature instabilities.

ℋpseudogap=ℋKLmf+ℋS​L​f+ℋY+ℰ2​[B,U]+ℰ4​[B,U]\mathcal{H}_{\rm pseudogap}=\mathcal{H}_{\rm KLmf}+\mathcal{H}_{SLf}+\mathcal{H}_{Y}+\mathcal{E}_{2}[B,U]+\mathcal{E}_{4}[B,U] (5.4)

specified in Eqs. (2.4), (3.2.1), (5.3), (4.17). This Hamiltonian has 3 fermions cαc_{\alpha}, f1​αf_{1\alpha}, fαf_{\alpha} whose transformations under SU(2) gauge, spin rotation, and electromagnetic charge symmetries are in Eqs. (4.8), (4.9), (4.10), with f1​αf_{1\alpha} transforming just like cαc_{\alpha}. As we noted earlier, the boson Φ\Phi will be treated as a cc-number constant for now, although we will consider its quantum and thermal fluctuations in Section 8 when we consider the transition to the FL phase at large doping. The completion of ℋpseudogap\mathcal{H}_{\rm pseudogap} for the case of dynamic Φ\Phi is presented in Appendix B.

The boson BB couples the Kondo Lattice to the spin liquid on the bottom layer, with SU(2) gauge field U𝒊​𝒋U_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}. If we ignore this couping, the Kondo lattice yields the ‘small’ heavy Fermi liquid Fermi surface of the FL* phase described in Section 2.2.4. Section 5.1 will consider fluctuations of BB to obtain a complete description of the electronic spectrum of the FL* phase. When BB condenses, we quench the SU(2) gauge field U𝒊​𝒋U_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}, and the resulting confining phases will be discussed in Section 6.

There is a remarkable similarity between Eq. (5.4), and the Weinberg-Salam theory of weak interactions [105]. Although the dispersions of the fermions and bosons have a lattice structure, the SU(2)×\times U(1) gauge structure (we treat the electromagnetic U(1) as global), and the Yukawa couplings between the Higgs and the fermions are similar, with the spinons mapping to neutrinos, and the electrons mapping to electrons.

5.1 Photoemission spectrum

In the mean-field analysis of Section 2.2.4, we obtained hole pocket description of the Fermi surface in Fig. 11, along with the dispersion antinodal pseudogap in Fig. 12. Here, we will consider modification of the Fermi surface from the coupling to the bottom layers of the ALM, where the spinons reside. Should the FL* state survive at T=0T=0, we expect the coupling of the hole pockets to the spinons to be relatively innocuous, as their interaction is mediated by the gapped BB bosons, and their zero energy modes lie at distinct momenta (see Fig. 22)—there remains a non-zero quasiparticle residue around the hole pocket at T=0T=0 [94].

However, there is a stronger effect at non-zero TT, above low TT phases (such as those in Fig. 23) where the spinons are confined. The computations of Pandey et al [125] of thermal fluctuations included the coupling to the spinons in ℋpseudogap\mathcal{H}_{\rm pseudogap} in Eq. (5.4). This can be expected to have a stronger effect along the Brillouin zone diagonals proximate to the spinon nodes, as shown in Fig. 22. Indeed they found that upon including thermal fluctuations the backside of the hole pockets are suppressed, and spectral weight turned into Fermi arcs, similar to observations.

They carried out Monte Carlo simulations of the classical, thermal, lattice gauge theory for BB and U𝒊​𝒋U_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}} defined by the partition function

𝒵2+0=∫∏i𝒟Bi∫∏⟨i​j⟩𝒟Ui​jexp(−(ℰ2[B,U]+ℰ4[B,U])/T),\mathcal{Z}_{2+0}=\int\prod_{i}\mathcal{D}B_{i}\int\prod_{\langle ij\rangle}\mathcal{D}U_{ij}\exp\left(-(\mathcal{E}_{2}[B,U]+\mathcal{E}_{4}[B,U])/T\right)\,, (5.5)

where the energy functionals are defined in Eq. (4.17). They observe a Kosterlitz-Thouless transition to a dd-wave superconductor at low energies. The choice of the coupling constants in ℰ4​[B,U]\mathcal{E}_{4}[B,U] was motivated by the phase diagram shown in Fig. 23: at the chosen point the ground state is a dd-wave superconductor, while the next best state has period 4 charge order.

Fig. 11 showed the prediction for the photoemission spectrum in the pseudogap phase without the coupling to the 𝑺2{\bm{S}}_{2} spin liquid. Pandey et al. [125] included the coupling to thermal fluctuations of BB via the Yukawa coupling in Eq. (5.3). The thermal fluctuations of BB and U𝒊​𝒋U_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}} were included via the ensemble in Eq. (5.5). Here the Born-Oppenheimer procedure is to choose random samples of the B𝒊B_{\bm{i}} and U𝒊​𝒋U_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}, diagonalize ℋKLmf+ℋS​L​f+ℋY\mathcal{H}_{\rm KLmf}+\mathcal{H}_{SLf}+\mathcal{H}_{Y} for each sample, and average over the spectral functions. The results are shown in Fig. 24.

Note that the back side of the pocket in Fig. 11 is now invisible, and the resulting spectrum is similar to the ‘Fermi arc’ observed in experiments.

5.2 Magnetotransport

With the success of the computation in Section 5.1, we need to return to the tension between these observations and the picture emerging from recent magnetotransport observations [11, 12] which favor hole pocket Fermi surfaces. In this section we discuss how this tension is resolved by a theory based upon ℋpseudogap\mathcal{H}_{\rm pseudogap} in Eq. (5.4).

Given the role of thermal BB fluctuations in removing the pocket backsides in the photoemission spectrum in Fig. 24, it is legitimate to ask if the thermal BB fluctuations will also wash out quantum oscillations. The latter probe does not eject electrons form the sample, unlike photoemission, and so its behavior can be distinct. This question was also investigated by Pandey et al. [125]: they averaged the quantum oscillations associated with ℋKLmf+ℋS​L​f+ℋY\mathcal{H}_{\rm KLmf}+\mathcal{H}_{SLf}+\mathcal{H}_{Y} over gaussian fluctations of BB. They found that the quantum oscillations are damped by thermal fluctuations but survive in regimes where the ‘back sides’ of the pockets are faint, as shown in Fig. 25.

6 From the pseudogap to dd-wave superconductivity and intertwined orders

This section addresses the fate of the FL* pseudogap as the temperature is lowered, upon including the coupling to the 𝑺2{\bm{S}}_{2} spin liquid in ℋpseudogap\mathcal{H}_{\rm pseudogap} in Eq. (5.4). This Hamiltonian specifically choses the π\pi-flux spin liquid of Section 3.2 for the 𝑺2{\bm{S}}_{2} layer. We will show that for this spin liquid there is a transition to a conventional BCS-type dd-wave superconductor, with anisotropic nodal velocities for the Boboliubov quasiparticles, and h/(2​e)h/(2e) vortices. Nevertheless the transition itself is not of the BCS type with a Cooper-pairing instability of a Fermi surface. Instead, the transition is driven by the confinement of the fractionalized excitations of the 𝑺2{\bm{S}}_{2} spin liquid. We also find nearby instabilities to charge ordering, consistent with observations. These instabilities are driven by the condensation of the Higgs field BB, which serves as a fractionalized order parameter whose composites describe the intertwined orders.

We note here recent numerics which support the idea of the dd-wave superconductor emerging from the doping-induced confinement of the π\pi-flux spin liquid. As we have discussed in Section 3.2, the π\pi-flux spin liquid is one description of the quantum-criticality between the Néel and VBS states. The numerical studies of Refs. [250, 251] examined the J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} square lattice antiferromagnet near the Néel-VBS transition, and indeed found dd-wave superconductivity upon doping.

6.1 Anisotropic velocities in the dd-wave superconductor

We now show how the problem of isotropic quasiparticle velocities, noted in Sections 1 and 4, is resolved by the presence of the pocket Fermi surfaces described by ℋKLmf\mathcal{H}_{\rm KLmf} in Eq. (2.4). The discussion below is based on the detailed computations presented in Refs. [130, 131].

Given the pocket Fermi surfaces and spinons in Fig. 22, we imagine imposing a BCS type pairing on the Fermi surface excitations. If the pairing is dd-wave, it would lead to 8 nodal Bogoliubov points as shown in Fig. 26A. However this state also has the 4 nodal quasiparticles of the 𝑺2{\bm{S}}_{2} spin liquid, associated with the dispersion in Fig. 16. So strictly speaking, this state remains fractionalized, and is not a conventional dd-wave superconductor. It would be appropriate to call it d-SC*.

However, if we induce the pairing by the BB condensate in Eq. (5.3), the SU(2) gauge field is higgsed. Morever, the Yukawa coupling allows the nodal quasiparticles of the 𝑺2{\bm{S}}_{2} spin liquid to hybridize with the Bogoliubov quasiparticles of the pocket Fermi surfaces. The net result, sketched in Fig. 26B, is that the BB condensate can enable the nodal points on the ‘backsides’ of the pocket Fermi surfaces to mutually annihilate with the spinons of the 𝑺2{\bm{S}}_{2} spin liquid. We are then left with the 4 nodal quasiparticles on front sides of the pocket Fermi surfaces. The number of nodal points are the same as those obtained in conventional BCS theory from dd-wave pairing of a Fermi liquid. These remaining nodal points are associated with pairing on the pocket Fermi surfaces, and these is no reason for their velocity to be isotropic (unlike the spinons).

We illustrate in Fig. 27 how this annihilation occurs via hybridization between the electrons and spinons within a mean-field band structure of ℋKLmf+ℋS​L​f+ℋY\mathcal{H}_{\rm KLmf}+\mathcal{H}_{SLf}+\mathcal{H}_{Y} in Eqs. (2.4), (3.2), and (5.3) .

Indeed, computations which diagonalize this Hamiltonian with BB fixed and U=1U=1 do indeed yield anisotropic velocities similar to those observed. Unlike the situation in Section 4, the spinons do not become the Bogoliubov quasiparticles in the doped case, although the spinons are needed to annihilate the extraneous Bogoliubov quasiparticles.

An interesting prediction can be made in the particular case of the electron-doped cuprates. In these materials, photoemission experiments have observed a normal state to superconductivity which is gapped near (π/2,π/2)(\pi/2,\pi/2) and has spectral weight only near electron pockets at the antinode [252]. If dd-wave superconductivity were to emerge as a BCS instability from such a normal state, the resulting superconductor should be gapped. However, the FL∗ theory yields a different prediction. Similar to how the spinon degrees of freedom emerge to annhilate with the backside pocket when BB Higgs condenses in the hole-doped case, the Dirac node of the spin liquid will appear with a finite spectral weight near (π/2,π/2)(\pi/2,\pi/2) when BB condenses, leading to a nodal superconductor, as shown in Fig. 28. Such a prediction can be explored in future photoemission experiments in the electron doped cuprates [253] and could serve as an experimental test of the FL∗ theory.

6.2 Vortices with flux h/(2​e)h/(2e) and charge order halos

We have seen in Sections 4 and 6.1 that dd-wave superconductivity is induced by the condensation of BB, a boson which carries electrical charge ee. So we might worry that the elementary flux quantum of such a superconductor is h/eh/e. However, that is not correct, and the SU(2) gauge field AμℓA^{\ell}_{\mu} (introduced in Eq. (3.52)) plays a central in establishing the presence of vortices with flux h/(2​e)h/(2e) [132].

The argument only requires AμzA^{z}_{\mu} to be non-zero. In terms of the two components of B=(B1,B2)B=(B_{1},B_{2}), we can write the following gradient term in the action far from the vortex core

|(∇−i​𝑨z−i​𝒂)​B1|2+|(∇+i​𝑨z−i​𝒂)​B2|2|({\bm{\nabla}}-i{\bm{A}}^{z}-i{\bm{a}})B_{1}|^{2}+|({\bm{\nabla}}+i{\bm{A}}^{z}-i{\bm{a}})B_{2}|^{2} (6.1)

where 𝑨z{\bm{A}}^{z} is the spatial component of AμzA^{z}_{\mu}, and 𝒂{\bm{a}} is the electromagnetic vector potential (we are using units here with ℏ=e=1\hbar=e=1). Let us assume that the phases of B1,2B_{1,2} wind by 2​π​n1,22\pi n_{1,2} around the vortex core, where n1,2n_{1,2} are integers. Then, finiteness of the energy of the vortex requires

∫d2​r​(∇×𝑨z+∇×𝒂)⋅𝒛^\displaystyle\int d^{2}r\,\left({\bm{\nabla}}\times{\bm{A}}^{z}+{\bm{\nabla}}\times{\bm{a}}\right)\cdot\hat{\bm{z}} =\displaystyle= 2​π​n1\displaystyle 2\pi n_{1}
∫d2​r​(∇×𝑨z−∇×𝒂)⋅𝒛^\displaystyle\int d^{2}r\,\left({\bm{\nabla}}\times{\bm{A}}^{z}-{\bm{\nabla}}\times{\bm{a}}\right)\cdot\hat{\bm{z}} =\displaystyle= 2​π​n2\displaystyle 2\pi n_{2} (6.2)

By choosing n1=1n_{1}=1, n2=0n_{2}=0, we obtain a vortex with ∫(∇×𝒂)⋅𝒛^=π\int\left({\bm{\nabla}}\times{\bm{a}}\right)\cdot\hat{\bm{z}}=\pi, which corresponds to flux h/(2​e)h/(2e).

There is an interesting feature of the vortex solution near its core. Recall from Eqs. (4.18,4.19) that different orientations of the complex vector (B1,B2)(B_{1},B_{2}) correspond to different local orders. At the vortex core, it is preferential for the orientation of BB to rotate from that preferring d-SC, to one of the other orders [132]. Explicit solutions of the continuum theory Eq. (4.20) were obtained in Ref. [132] with period 2 charge order.

Fig. 29 shows a snapshot from the simulation of Ref. [125] at low TT at the parameter value in Fig. 23.

Note the vortices with the phase winding of 2​π2\pi in the superconducting order parameter (corresponding to h/(2​e)h/(2e) vortices), and the period 4 charge order halos around each vortex. These halos are remarkably similar to those observed by Hoffman et al. [133]. Several other features of the vortex solution were also found in Ref. [132] to correspond STM observations.

6.3 Quantum oscillations

We discussed observations in high magnetic field in the intermediate temperature pseudogap phase in Section 5.2. Here we turn to observations at very low TT.

At large doping, Vignolle et al. [30] observed quantum oscillations are compatible with a ‘large’ Fermi surface of area (1+p)/2(1+p)/2.

At low doping and low temperatures, quantum oscillations show evidence for small electron pockets [134]. The formation of electron pockets is believed to be associated with the appearance of charge density wave order at high magnetic fields. But computations on charge density wave models had difficulty reproducing the observed spectrum.

Harrison and Sebastian [254] proposed a phenomenological model of the electron pocket, in which the Fermi arcs combined to form an α\alpha electron pocket after shifts by the wavevectors of the charge density wave (CDW). This is illustrated in Fig. 30

Zhang and Mei [255] worked with a model of pocket Fermi surfaces (similar to ℋKLmf\mathcal{H}_{\rm KLmf}) in the presence of CDW order: in addition to the observed α\alpha electron pocket, their results show an unobserved additional oscillation frequency from a β\beta Fermi surface arising from the backsides of the hole pockets completing the Fermi arcs. This is illustrated in Fig. 31a. Note that this computation leads to a CDW* state, because the spinons remain deconfined.

Bonetti et al. [135] extended the computations of Zhang and Mei to include spinons by working with ℋKLmf+ℋS​L​f+ℋY\mathcal{H}_{\rm KLmf}+\mathcal{H}_{SLf}+\mathcal{H}_{Y} in Eqs. (2.4), (3.2.1), (5.3). They included the charge density wave by a BB condensate which had spatial modulations but no superconducting order, as defined by the local mappings in Eq. (4.18). The presence of the BB condensate implies that the SU(2) gauge field is fully higgsed, and the resulting state is a conventional CDW with no fractionalized excitations. As shown in Fig. 31b, the unobserved β\beta pocket is replaced by the δ\delta pockets which are very small and hence compatible with current quantum oscillation data. The role of the spinons here in removing unobserved fermionic excitaions is rather analogous to their role in Sections 5.1 and 6.1.

7 The SYK model

We now turn to a different critical quantum liquid, associated with mobile electrons, the SYK model. This is a zero-dimensional model for which the absence of quasiparticle excitations is well-established. A direct and extensive application of the zero-dimensional SYK model has been to the low energy quantum theory of charged black holes, and this is reviewed elsewhere [256]. There are also connections to experiments on graphene flakes [257, 258]. But our primary interest here will be extensions to two-dimensional models relevant to the strange metal state of the cuprates and other correlated electron materials—we will turn to this in Section 8, where the zero-dimensional SYK models will motivate a theory of realistic FL*-FL transitions in two-dimensional metals. We also note other reviews [136, 137, 138] for a more in-depth discussion of the topics in Sections 7-9.

The Hamiltonian of a version of a SYK model is illustrated in Fig. 32. A system with fermions c𝒊c_{\bm{i}}, i=1​…​Ni=1\ldots N states is assumed. Depending upon physical realizations, the label 𝒊{\bm{i}} could be position or an orbital, and it is best to just think of it as an abstract label of a fermionic qubit with the two states |0⟩\left|0\right\rangle and c𝒊†|0⟩c_{\bm{i}}^{\dagger}\left|0\right\rangle. 𝒬​N\mathcal{Q}N fermions are placed in these states, so that a density 𝒬≈1/2\mathcal{Q}\approx 1/2 is occupied, as shown in Fig. 32.

The quantum dynamics is restricted to only have a ‘collision’ term between the fermions, analogous to the right-hand-side of the Boltzmann equation. However, in stark contrast to the Boltzmann equation, statistically independent collisions are not assumed, and quantum interference between successive collisions is accounted for: this is the key to building up a many-body state with non-trivial entanglement. So a collision in which fermions move from sites 𝒊{\bm{i}} and jj to sites kk and ℓ\ell is characterized not by a probability, but by a quantum amplitude U𝒊​𝒋;k​ℓU_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}};k\ell}, which is a complex number.

The model so defined has a Hilbert space of order 2N2^{N} states, and a Hamiltonian determined by order N4N^{4} numbers U𝒊​𝒋;k​ℓU_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}};k\ell}. Determining the spectrum or dynamics of such a Hamiltonian for large NN seems like an impossibly formidable task. But with the assumption that the U𝒊​𝒋;k​ℓU_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}};k\ell} are statistically independent random numbers, remarkable progress is possible. Note that an ensemble of SYK models with different U𝒊​𝒋;k​ℓU_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}};k\ell} is not being considered, but a single fixed set of U𝒊​𝒋;k​ℓU_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}};k\ell}. Most physical properties of this model are self-averaging at large NN, and so as a technical tool, they can be rapidly obtained by computations on an ensemble of random U𝒊​𝒋;k​ℓU_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}};k\ell}. In any case, the analytic results described below have been checked by numerical computations on a computer for a fixed set of U𝒊​𝒋;k​ℓU_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}};k\ell}. Recall that, even for the Boltzmann equation, there was an ensemble average over the initial positions and momenta of the molecules that was implicitly performed.

Specifically, the Hamiltonian in a chemical potential μ\mu is

ℋ=1(2​N)3/2​∑𝒊,𝒋,k,ℓ=1NU𝒊​𝒋;k​ℓ​c𝒊†​c𝒋†​ck​cℓ−μ​∑𝒊c𝒊†​c𝒊\displaystyle\mathcal{H}=\frac{1}{(2N)^{3/2}}\sum_{{\bm{i}},{\bm{j}},k,\ell=1}^{N}U_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}};k\ell}\,c_{\bm{i}}^{\dagger}c_{\bm{j}}^{\dagger}c_{k}^{\vphantom{\dagger}}c_{\ell}^{\vphantom{\dagger}}-\mu\sum_{{\bm{i}}}c_{\bm{i}}^{\dagger}c_{\bm{i}}^{\vphantom{\dagger}}
c𝒊​c𝒋+c𝒋​c𝒊=0,c𝒊​c𝒋†+c𝒋†​c𝒊=δ𝒊​𝒋\displaystyle~~~~~~c_{\bm{i}}c_{\bm{j}}+c_{\bm{j}}c_{\bm{i}}=0\quad,\quad c_{\bm{i}}^{\vphantom{\dagger}}c_{\bm{j}}^{\dagger}+c_{\bm{j}}^{\dagger}c_{\bm{i}}^{\vphantom{\dagger}}=\delta_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}
𝒬=1N​∑𝒊c𝒊†​c𝒊;[ℋ,𝒬]=0;0≤𝒬≤1,\displaystyle~~~~\mathcal{Q}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\bm{i}}c_{\bm{i}}^{\dagger}c_{\bm{i}}^{\vphantom{\dagger}}\,;\quad[\mathcal{H},\mathcal{Q}]=0\,;\quad 0\leq\mathcal{Q}\leq 1\,, (7.1)

and its large NN limit is most simply taken graphically, order-by-order in U𝒊​𝒋;k​ℓU_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}};k\ell}, and averaging over U𝒊​𝒋;k​ℓU_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}};k\ell} as independent random variables with U𝒊​𝒋;k​ℓ¯=0\overline{U_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}};k\ell}}=0 and |U𝒊​𝒋;k​ℓ|2¯=U2\overline{|U_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}};k\ell}|^{2}}=U^{2}.

This expansion can be used to compute graphically the Green’s function in imaginary time τ\tau

G(τ)=−1N∑𝒊⟨𝒯⁡(c𝒊​(τ)​c𝒊†​(0))⟩¯,\displaystyle G(\tau)=-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\bm{i}}\overline{\left\langle\mathcal{T}\left(c_{\bm{i}}(\tau)c_{\bm{i}}^{\dagger}(0)\right)\right\rangle}\,, (7.2)

where 𝒯\mathcal{T} is the time-ordering symbol, the angular brackets are a quantum average for any given U𝒊​𝒋;k​ℓU_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}};k\ell}, and the over-line denotes an average over the ensemble of U𝒊​𝒋;k​ℓU_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}};k\ell}. (It turns out that the last average is not needed for large NN, because the quantum observable is self-averaging.) In the large NN limit, only the graph for the Dyson self energy, Σ\Sigma, in Fig. 33 survives, and the on-site fermion Green’s function is given by the solution of the following equations

G⁡(i​ωn)\displaystyle G(i\omega_{n}) =1i​ωn+μ−Σ⁡(i​ωn)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{i\omega_{n}+\mu-\Sigma(i\omega_{n})}
Σ⁡(τ)\displaystyle\Sigma(\tau) =−U2​G2​(τ)​G​(−τ)\displaystyle=-U^{2}G^{2}(\tau)G(-\tau)
G⁡(τ=0−)\displaystyle G(\tau=0^{-}) =𝒬,\displaystyle=\mathcal{Q}\,, (7.3)

where ωn\omega_{n} is a fermionic Matsubara frequency. The first equation in Eq. (7.3) is the usual Dyson relation between the Green’s function and self energy in quantum field theory, the second equation in Eq. (7.3) is the Feynman graph in Fig. 33, and the last determines the chemical potential μ\mu from the charge density 𝒬\mathcal{Q}. These equations can also be obtained as saddle-point equations of the following exact representation of the disordered-averaged partition function, expressed as a ‘G−ΣG-\Sigma’ theory [259, 260, 261, 262]:

𝒵\displaystyle\mathcal{Z} =∫𝒟​G​(τ1,τ2)​𝒟​Σ​(τ1,τ2)​exp⁡(−N​I)\displaystyle=\int\mathcal{D}G(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})\mathcal{D}\Sigma(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})\exp(-NI)
I\displaystyle I =lndet[δ(τ1−τ2)(∂τ1+μ)−Σ(τ1,τ2)]\displaystyle=\ln\det\left[\delta(\tau_{1}-\tau_{2})(\partial_{\tau_{1}}+\mu)-\Sigma(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})\right] (7.4)
+∫dτ1dτ2[Σ(τ1,τ2)G(τ2,τ1)+(U2/2)G2(τ2,τ1)G2(τ1,τ2)]\displaystyle~~~+\int d\tau_{1}d\tau_{2}\left[\Sigma(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})G(\tau_{2},\tau_{1})+(U^{2}/2)G^{2}(\tau_{2},\tau_{1})G^{2}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})\right]

This is a path-integral over bi-local in time functions G⁡(τ1,τ2)G(\tau_{1},\tau_{2}) and Σ⁡(τ1,τ2)\Sigma(\tau_{1},\tau_{2}), whose saddle point values are the Green’s function G⁡(τ1−τ2)G(\tau_{1}-\tau_{2}), and the self energy Σ⁡(τ1−τ2)\Sigma(\tau_{1}-\tau_{2}). This bi-local GG can be viewed as a composite quantum operator corresponding to an on-site fermion bilinear

G(τ1,τ2)=−1N∑𝒊𝒯(c𝒊(τ1)c𝒊†(τ2))\displaystyle G(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})=-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\bm{i}}\mathcal{T}\left(c_{\bm{i}}(\tau_{1})c_{\bm{i}}^{\dagger}(\tau_{2})\right) (7.5)

that is averaged in Eq. (7.2).

For general ω\omega and TT, the equations in Eq. (7.3) have to be solved numerically. But an exact analytic solution is possible in the limit ω,T≪U\omega,T\ll U. At T=0T=0, the asymptotic forms can be obtained straightforwardly [14]

G(iω)∼−isgn(ω)|ω|−1/2,Σ(iω)−Σ(0)∼−isgn(ω)|ω|1/2,\displaystyle G(i\omega)\sim-i\mbox{sgn}(\omega)|\omega|^{-1/2}\quad,\quad\Sigma(i\omega)-\Sigma(0)\sim-i\mbox{sgn}(\omega)|\omega|^{1/2}\,, (7.6)

and a more complete analysis of Eq. (7.3) gives the exact form at non-zero TT (ℏ=kB=1\hbar=k_{B}=1) [263]

G⁡(ω)=−i​C​e−i​θ(2​π​T)1/2​Γ⁡(14−i​ω2​π​T+i​ℰ)Γ⁡(34−i​ω2​π​T+i​ℰ)|ω|,T≪U.\displaystyle G(\omega)=\frac{-iCe^{-i\theta}}{(2\pi T)^{1/2}}\frac{\Gamma\left(\displaystyle\frac{1}{4}-\frac{i\omega}{2\pi T}+i\mathcal{E}\right)}{\Gamma\left(\displaystyle\frac{3}{4}-\frac{i\omega}{2\pi T}+i\mathcal{E}\right)}\quad\quad|\omega|,T\ll U\,. (7.7)

Here, ℰ\mathcal{E} is a dimensionless number which characterizes the particle-hole asymmetry of the spectral function; both ℰ\mathcal{E} and the pre-factor CC are determined by an angle −π/4<θ<π/4-\pi/4<\theta<\pi/4

e2​π​ℰ=sin⁡(π/4+θ)sin⁡(π/4−θ),C=(πU2​cos⁡(2​θ))1/4,\displaystyle e^{2\pi\mathcal{E}}=\frac{\sin(\pi/4+\theta)}{\sin(\pi/4-\theta)}\quad,\quad C=\left(\frac{\pi}{U^{2}\cos(2\theta)}\right)^{1/4}\,, (7.8)

and the value of θ\theta is determined by a Luttinger relation to the density 𝒬\mathcal{Q} [259]

𝒬=12−θπ−sin⁡(2​θ)4.\displaystyle\mathcal{Q}=\frac{1}{2}-\frac{\theta}{\pi}-\frac{\sin(2\theta)}{4}\,. (7.9)

A notable property of Eq. (7.7) at ℰ=0\mathcal{E}=0 is that it equals the temporal Fourier transform of the spatially local correlator of a fermionic field of dimension 1/4 in a conformal field theory in 1+1 spacetime dimensions. A theory in 0+1 dimensions is considered here, where conformal transformations map the temporal circle onto itself, as reviewed in Appendices A and B of Ref. [136]; such transformations allow a non-zero ℰ\mathcal{E}. An important consequence of this conformal invariance is that Eq. (7.7) is a scaling function of ℏ​ω/(kB​T)\hbar\omega/(k_{B}T) (after restoring fundamental constants); in other words, the characteristic frequency scale of Eq. (7.7) is determined solely by kB​T/ℏk_{B}T/\hbar, and is independent of the value of U/ℏU/\hbar. A careful study of the consequences of this conformal invariance have established the following properties of the SYK model (more complete references to the literature are given in other reviews [136, 7]):

  • •

    There are no quasiparticle excitations, and the SYK model exhibits quantum dynamics with a Planckian relaxation time of order ℏ/(kB​T)\hbar/(k_{B}T) at T≪UT\ll U. In particular, the relaxation time is independent of UU, a feature not present in any ordinary metal with quasiparticles. While the Planckian relaxation in Eq. (7.7) implies the absence of quasiparticles with the same quantum numbers as the cc fermion, it does not rule out the possibility that cc has fractionalized into some emergent quasiparticles; this possibility is ruled out by the exponentially large number of low energy states, as discussed below.

  • •

    At large NN, the many-body density of states at fixed 𝒬\mathcal{Q} is [264, 265, 262, 261, 266, 267] (see Fig. 34a)

    D⁡(E)∼1N​exp⁡(N​s0)​sinh⁡(2​N​γ​E),D(E)\sim\frac{1}{N}\exp(Ns_{0})\sinh\left(\sqrt{2N\gamma E}\right)\,, (7.10)

    where the ground state energy has been set to zero. Here s0s_{0} is a universal number dependent only on 𝒬\mathcal{Q} (s0=0.4648476991708051​…s_{0}=0.4648476991708051\ldots for 𝒬=1/2\mathcal{Q}=1/2), γ∼1/U\gamma\sim 1/U is the only parameter dependent upon the strength of the interactions, and the NN dependence of the pre-factor is discussed in Ref. [267].

    Given D⁡(E)D(E), the partition function can be computed from

    𝒵(T)=∫dED(E)e−E/(kBT),\mathcal{Z}(T)=\int dED(E)e^{-E/(k_{B}T)}\,, (7.11)

    and hence the low-TT dependence of the entropy at fixed QQ is given by

    S⁡(T)kB=N⁡(s0+γ​kB​T)−32​ln⁡(UkB​T)−ln⁡N2+….\frac{S(T)}{k_{B}}=N(s_{0}+\gamma\,k_{B}T)-\frac{3}{2}\ln\left(\frac{U}{k_{B}T}\right)-\frac{\ln N}{2}+\ldots\,. (7.12)

    The thermodynamic limit limN→∞S⁡(T)/N\lim_{N\rightarrow\infty}S(T)/N yields the microcanonical entropy

    S⁡(E)/kB=N​s0+2​N​γ​E,\displaystyle S(E)/k_{B}=Ns_{0}+\sqrt{2N\gamma E}\,, (7.13)

    and this connects to the extensive EE limit of Eq. (7.10) after using Boltzmann’s formula D⁡(E)∼exp⁡(S⁡(E)/kB)D(E)\sim\exp\left(S(E)/k_{B}\right). The limit limT→0limN→∞S⁡(T)/(kB​N)=s0\lim_{T\rightarrow 0}\lim_{N\rightarrow\infty}S(T)/(k_{B}N)=s_{0} is non-zero, implying an energy-level spacing exponentially small in NN near the ground state: the density of states Eq. (7.10) implies that any small energy interval near the ground state contains an exponentially large number of energy eigenstates (see Fig. 34a). This is very different from systems with quasiparticle excitations, whose energy level spacing vanishes with a positive power of 1/N1/N near the ground state, as quasiparticles have order NN quantum numbers. The exponentially small level spacing therefore rules out the existence of quasiparticles in the SYK model.

  • •

    However, it important to note that there is no exponentially large degeneracy of the ground state itself in the SYK model, unlike that in a supersymmetric generalization of the SYK model (see Fig. 34b) and the ground states in Pauling’s model of ice [269]. Indeed, the SYK model is the first system to exhibit an extensive zero temperature entropy without an exponentially large ground state degeneracy. Obtaining the ground-state degeneracy requires the opposite order of limits between TT and NN, and numerical studies show that the entropy density does vanish in such a limit for the SYK model. The many-particle wavefunctions of the low-energy eigenstates in Fock space change chaotically from one state to the next, providing a realization of maximal many-body quantum chaos [270] in a precise sense. This structure of eigenstates is very different from systems with quasiparticles, for which the lowest energy eigenstates differ only by adding and removing a few quasiparticles.

  • •

    The EE dependence of the density of states in Eq. (7.10) is associated with a time reparameterization mode, and Eq. (7.10) shows that its effects are important when E∼1/NE\sim 1/N. The low energy quantum fluctuations of Eq. (7.4) can be expressed in terms of a path integral which reparameterizes imaginary time τ→f⁡(τ)\tau\rightarrow f(\tau), in a manner analogous to the quantum theory of gravity being expressed in terms of the fluctuations of the spacetime metric. There are also quantum fluctuations of a phase mode ϕ⁡(τ)\phi(\tau), whose time derivative is the charge density, and the path integral in Eq. (7.4) reduces to the partition function

    𝒵S​Y​K−T​R=eN​s0∫𝒟f𝒟ϕexp(−1ℏ∫0ℏ/(kB​T)dτℒS​Y​K−T​R[f,ϕ])\mathcal{Z}_{SYK-TR}=e^{Ns_{0}}\int\mathcal{D}f\mathcal{D}\phi\exp\left(-\frac{1}{\hbar}\int_{0}^{\hbar/(k_{B}T)}\!\!\!\!\!\!d\tau\,\mathcal{L}_{SYK-TR}[f,\phi]\right) (7.14)

    The Lagrangian ℒS​Y​K−T​R\mathcal{L}_{SYK-TR} is known, and involves a Schwarzian of f⁡(τ)f(\tau). Remarkably, despite its non-quadratic Lagrangian, the path integral in Eq. (7.14) can be performed exactly [266], and leads to Eq. (7.10).

7.1 The Yukawa-SYK model

The SYK model defined above is a 0+1 dimensional theory with no spatial structure, and so cannot be directly applied to transport of strange metals in non-zero spatial dimensions. A great deal of work has been undertaken on generalizing the SYK model to non-zero spatial dimensions [136], but this effort has ultimately not been successful: although ‘bad metal’ states (see Section 8) have been obtained, low TT strange metals have not. But another effort based upon a variation of the SYK model, the 0+1 dimensional ‘Yukawa-SYK’ model [268, 271, 272, 273, 274, 275, 276, 277, 278, 279, 280, 281], has been a much better starting point for a non-zero spatial dimensional theory, as shown in Section 8.

In the spirit of Eq. (7.1), a model of fermions c𝒊c_{\bm{i}} (i=1​…​Ni=1\ldots N) and bosons Φℓ\Phi_{\ell} (ℓ=1​…​N\ell=1\ldots N) with a Yukawa coupling g𝒊​𝒋​ℓg_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}\ell} between them is now considered

ℋY=−μ∑𝒊c𝒊†c𝒊+∑ℓ12(πℓ2+ω02Φℓ2)+1N∑𝒊​𝒋​ℓg𝒊​𝒋​ℓc𝒊†c𝒋Φℓ,\displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{Y}=-\mu\sum_{{\bm{i}}}c_{\bm{i}}^{\dagger}c_{\bm{i}}^{\vphantom{\dagger}}+\sum_{\ell}\frac{1}{2}\left(\pi_{\ell}^{2}+\omega_{0}^{2}\Phi_{\ell}^{2}\right)+\frac{1}{N}\sum_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}\ell}g_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}\ell}^{\vphantom{\dagger}}c_{\bm{i}}^{\dagger}c_{\bm{j}}^{\vphantom{\dagger}}\Phi_{\ell}^{\vphantom{\dagger}}\,, (7.15)

with g𝒊​𝒋​ℓg_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}\ell} independent random numbers with zero mean and r.m.s. value gg. The bosons are oscillators with the same frequency ω0\omega_{0}, while the fermions have no one-particle hopping. The large NN limit of Eq. (7.15) can be taken just as for the SYK model in Eq. (7.1). The self-energy graph in Fig. 33 is replaced by those in Fig. 35: the phonon Green’s function is DD, while the phonon self-energy is Π\Pi.

Continuing the parallel with the SYK model, the disorder-averaged partition function of the Yukawa-SYK model is a bi-local GG-Σ\Sigma-DD-Π\Pi theory, analogous to Eq. (7.4):

𝒵\displaystyle\mathcal{Z} =∫𝒟​G​𝒟​Σ​𝒟​D​𝒟​Π​exp⁡(−N​Sall)\displaystyle=\int\mathcal{D}G\,\mathcal{D}\Sigma\,\mathcal{D}D\,\mathcal{D}\Pi\exp(-NS_{\rm all})
Sall\displaystyle S_{\rm all} =−lndet(∂τ−μ+Σ)+12lndet(−∂τ2+ω02−Π)\displaystyle=-\ln\det(\partial_{\tau}-\mu+\Sigma)+\frac{1}{2}\ln\det(-\partial_{\tau}^{2}+\omega_{0}^{2}-\Pi) (7.16)
+∫dτ∫dτ′[−Σ(τ′;τ)G(τ,τ′)+12Π(τ′,τ)D(τ,τ′)\displaystyle+\int d\tau\int d\tau^{\prime}\left[-\Sigma(\tau^{\prime};\tau)G(\tau,\tau^{\prime})+\frac{1}{2}\Pi(\tau^{\prime},\tau)D(\tau,\tau^{\prime})\right.
+g22G(τ,τ′)G(τ′,τ)D(τ,τ′)].\displaystyle~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~\left.+\frac{g^{2}}{2}G(\tau,\tau^{\prime})G(\tau^{\prime},\tau)D(\tau,\tau^{\prime})\right]\,.

The large NN saddle-point equations replacing Eq. (7.3) are:

G⁡(i​ωn)=1i​ωn+μ−Σ⁡(i​ωn)\displaystyle G(i\omega_{n})=\frac{1}{i\omega_{n}+\mu-\Sigma(i\omega_{n})}\quad ,D(iωn)=1ωn2+ω02−Π⁡(i​ωn)\displaystyle,\quad D(i\omega_{n})=\frac{1}{\omega_{n}^{2}+\omega_{0}^{2}-\Pi(i\omega_{n})}
Σ⁡(τ)=g2​G​(τ)​D​(τ)\displaystyle\Sigma(\tau)=g^{2}G(\tau)D(\tau)\quad ,Π(τ)=−g2G(τ)G(−τ)\displaystyle,\quad\Pi(\tau)=-g^{2}G(\tau)G(-\tau) (7.17)

The solution of Eqs. (7.16) and (7.17) leads to a critical state with properties very similar to that of the SYK model [275, 279, 280, 281]. Only the low-frequency behavior of the Green’s functions at T=0T=0, is quoted analogous to Eq. (7.6):

G⁡(i​ω)∼−i​sgn​(ω)​|ω|−(1−2​Δ),D⁡(i​ω)∼|ω|1−4​Δ,14<Δ<12.\displaystyle G(i\omega)\sim-i\mbox{sgn}(\omega)|\omega|^{-(1-2\Delta)}\quad,\quad D(i\omega)\sim|\omega|^{1-4\Delta}\quad,\quad\frac{1}{4}<\Delta<\frac{1}{2}\,. (7.18)

Inserting the ansatz Eq. (7.18) into Eq. (7.17) fixes the value of the critical exponent Δ\Delta.

4​Δ−12​(2​Δ−1)​[sec⁡(2​π​Δ)−1]=1,Δ=0.42037​…\displaystyle\frac{4\Delta-1}{2(2\Delta-1)[\sec(2\pi\Delta)-1]}=1\quad,\quad\Delta=0.42037\ldots (7.19)

Although the fermion Green’s function has an exponent which differs from that of the SYK model, the thermodynamic properties have the same structure as that of the SYK model, including the presence of the Schwarzian mode and the form of the many-body density of states.

8 From the SYK model to strange metals

We now turn to the ‘strange metal’ regime of Fig. 1 and 2. A similar regime is found in numerous correlated electron materials, and we will present here a theory [139, 169] which applies to a wide variety of quantum phase transitions, and so can explain the universality in the observations.

Some of the key properties of strange metals, as observed in recent experiments, are first summarized [282]:

  1. 1.

    The resistivity, ρ⁡(T)\rho(T), of strange metals has a linear-TT dependence at low temperatures:

    ρ⁡(T)=ρ0+A​T+…,T→0.\displaystyle\rho(T)=\rho_{0}+AT+\ldots\quad,\quad T\rightarrow 0. (8.1)

    Importantly, this resistivity is below the Mott-Ioffe-Regel bound [282], so ρ⁡(T)<h/e2\rho(T)<h/e^{2} in d=2d=2 spatial dimensions. Metals with ρ⁡(T)>h/e2\rho(T)>h/e^{2} are bad metals, and are not discussed here. Bad metals can be described by lattice models of coupled SYK ‘islands’ [283, 284, 162], as reviewed elsewhere [136].

  2. 2.

    Ordinary metals have low TT specific heat which vanishes linearly with TT, but in a strange metal the specific heat is enhanced to ∼T​ln⁡(1/T)\sim T\ln(1/T) as T→0T\rightarrow 0.

  3. 3.

    Careful analyses of optical data in the cuprates over wide ranges of frequencies and temperatures [285, 286] has shown that the optical conductivity can be accurately described by the following form

    σ⁡(ω)=K1τtrans​(ω)−i​ω​mtrans∗​(ω)m;1τtrans​(ω)∼|ω|​Φσ​(ℏ​ωkB​T),\displaystyle\sigma(\omega)=\frac{K}{\displaystyle\frac{1}{\tau_{\rm trans}(\omega)}-i\omega\frac{m_{\rm trans}^{\ast}(\omega)}{m}}~~;~~\frac{1}{\tau_{\rm trans}(\omega)}\sim|\omega|\Phi_{\sigma}\left(\frac{\hbar\omega}{k_{B}T}\right)\,, (8.2)

    where KK is a constant, and the transport scattering rate 1/τtrans1/\tau_{\rm trans} scales linearly with the larger of |ω||\omega| and kB​T/ℏk_{B}T/\hbar. The frequency dependence of the effective transport mass mtrans∗m_{\rm trans}^{\ast} is then determined by a Kramers-Kronig connection to that of 1/τtrans1/\tau_{\rm trans}, which leads to a logarithmic frequency dependence in mtrans∗​(ω)m_{\rm trans}^{\ast}(\omega).

  4. 4.

    Photoemission experiments on the cuprates have measured the electron self-energy near the nodal point in the Brillouin zone. This was found to obey the scaling form [182]

    1τin​(ω)=2​Im​Σ​(ω)∼|ω|2​α​ΦΣ​(ℏ​ωkB​T)\displaystyle\frac{1}{\tau_{\rm in}(\omega)}=2\,\mbox{Im}\Sigma(\omega)\sim|\omega|^{2\alpha}\Phi_{\Sigma}\left(\frac{\hbar\omega}{k_{B}T}\right) (8.3)

    with an exponent α≈1/2\alpha\approx 1/2 near optimal doping. The value α=1/2\alpha=1/2 corresponds to a ‘marginal Fermi liquid’ [287], at least as far as the self energy is concerned. But an important point is that there is no direct theoretical connection between the single-particle scattering rate 1/τin​(ω)1/\tau_{\rm in}(\omega) in Eq. (8.3), and the value of transport scattering rate 1/τtrans​(ω)1/\tau_{\rm trans}(\omega) in Eq. (8.2), although they are observed to have the same exponent. As seen below, the transport and single-particle scattering rates can be very different in some common models.

  5. 5.

    In experimental observations [288, 289, 290], the value of the overall constant KK in Eq. (8.2) is often fixed by writing the d.c. conductivity in the Drude form

    σ=n​e2​τtransm∗,\displaystyle\sigma=\frac{ne^{2}\tau_{\rm trans}}{m^{\ast}}\,, (8.4)

    where nn is the known conduction electron density, and m∗m^{\ast} is an electronic effective mass. In some experiments, the transport mass mtrans∗m_{\rm trans}^{\ast} of Eq. (8.2) is used in Eq. (8.4), while other experiments use the m∗m^{\ast} determined from thermodynamic measurements. In the form Eq. (8.4), the absolute value of τtrans\tau_{\rm trans} can be deduced from experimental observations. In the strange metal, such a value is found to obey ‘Planckian’ behavior with [288, 289, 290, 291, 292, 293, 294]

    1τtrans=α~​kB​Tℏ,\displaystyle\frac{1}{\tau_{\rm trans}}=\widetilde{\alpha}\,\frac{k_{B}T}{\hbar}\,, (8.5)

with α~\widetilde{\alpha} a numerical constant of order unity. Measurements of 1/τtrans1/\tau_{\rm trans} in La1.6-xNd0.4SrxCuO4 in angle-dependent magnetotransport show α~=1.2±0.4\widetilde{\alpha}=1.2\pm 0.4 [290] upon using the thermodynamic m∗m^{\ast}.

8.1 Universal model

This subsection will present a simple and universal generalization of the Yukawa-SYK model of Section 7.1 to spatial dimension d=2d=2 which reproduces all five of the above observed properties [139, 169].

We will discuss the model appropriate for the cuprates here, although the results can be extended to other metallic quantum phase transitions with or without disorder. As we have noted in Section 1.2, in the clean case when umklapp scattering is suppressed, although there can be no quasiparticles around the Fermi surface, the transport is nevertheless Fermi liquid-like: this will be described in Section 8.2. So we will focus on the disordered case, with the most important disorder being of the Harris type, which produces local variations in the value of the coupling tuning the system across the quantum critical point.

Our model for the hole-doped cuprates is a FL*-FL quantum phase transition (see Fig. 37) without symmetry breaking, and in the clean limit this is distinct from metallic quantum phase transitions with symmetry breaking. The latter are further distinguished in the clean limit by cases in which the order parameters reside at zero or non-zero momenta [18] which have dynamic critical exponents z=3z=3 and z=2z=2 respectively. The remarkable fact is that spatial disorder unifies these 3 classes into essentially the same universal theory [139] which we summarize below for the case of the FL*-FL transition, and in Section 9 for the spin density wave transitions. However, we note that there is an enhancement of thermopower which is special to the FL*-FL transition, as discussed elsewhere [171], and this compares well with experiments on the cuprates [172, 173, 174].

For the cuprates, we present the phase diagram of Fig. 2 again in Fig. 36, but now with annotations updated with reference to the ALM in Fig. 21.

In Section 6 we have considered the low temperature fate of the FL* pseudogap associated with condensation of the Higgs field BB. In this analysis, we treated Φ\Phi simply as a c-number constant. In the present section, Φ\Phi and BB will exchange roles. In considering the transition from FL* to FL in Fig. 8 and Fig. 36, we consider the dynamics of the Φ\Phi field, and the fermions in the top two layers in Fig. 21. In FL*, we can safely set B=0B=0 (apart for some thermal fluctuations which were needed in Section 5.1). In the FL phase of Fig. 8, we see that the f1f_{1} fermions of the middle layer form a trivial rung-singlet state with the ff fermions in the bottom layer: this confinement of f1f_{1} and ff is not associated with BB, but by the confinement of a SU~​(2)\widetilde{\rm SU}(2) gauge field [4, 140, 218] (see Appendix B). Consequently, it is safe to ignore BB in the quantum criticality of the FL* to FL transition [4, 140, 295]. So we will only consider the Φ\Phi boson here, along with the cαc_{\alpha} and f1f_{1} fermions in the top two layers of the ALM.

We therefore consider the T>0T>0 quantum criticality of the FL* to FL transition [2, 3] sketched in Fig. 37, associated with the Higgs transition in Φ\Phi [4]. Note that Φ\Phi was also the key variational parameter in the trial wavefunction description of the FL* to FL transition in Section 2.2.3.

Dynamic mean-field theories. We could study this transition using the dynamic mean field theories [14, 136, 146, 147, 148, 19, 20, 149, 150, 151, 152, 153, 154, 155, 70, 156, 21, 157, 158, 159, 160, 161], which map the transition to self-consistent Green’s functions similar to those studied in Section 7. Such theories are in the strong umklapp limit, and could apply in very clean Kondo lattice systems over a significant intermediate temperature range. However, we expect umklapp to be suppressed at low temperatures, and the emergence of a conserved momentum leads to absence of strange metal behavior, as we discuss in Section 8.2; similar comments apply to other numerical studies [296, 297]. Moreover, the dynamic mean-field theories also have the serious issue of a non-vanishing entropy density in the zero temperature limit [136].

Here, we will instead treat the spatial dimensionality seriously, and focus on the low energy, long-wavelength structure. Spatially random couplings play a crucial role in such an analysis, and lead to new Griffiths effects associated with the ‘foot’ of strange metal behavior [177, 178, 138] which we will discuss in Section 9.

As an aside, we note that the FL*-FL quantum critical point is expected to be unstable to dd-wave superconductivity [4, 140], with the BCS state on the FL side adiabatically connected to the superconductivity obtained from FL*, as we have seen in Sections 4 and 2. So the FL*-FL quantum critical point will disappear under the superconducting dome, as shown earlier in Fig. 1. This is an important distinction from quantum transitions in metals with symmetry breaking: then there are two distinct superconducting states, and the symmetry breaking transition is also present within the superconducting dome.

At the mean-field level the FL* to FL transition is described by ℋKLmf\mathcal{H}_{\rm KLmf} in Eq. (2.4). Starting from ℋKLmf\mathcal{H}_{\rm KLmf}, we include spatial dependence in all fields, allow for quenched spatial disorder, and obtain the (universal) Lagrangian of the two-dimensional Yukawa-Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev (2D-YSYK) model

ℒΦ\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\Phi} =∑𝒌c𝒌​α†​(∂∂τ+ε⁡(𝒌))​c𝒌​α+∑𝒌f1​𝒌​α†​(∂∂τ+ε1​(𝒌))​f1​𝒌​α\displaystyle=\sum_{\bm{k}}c_{{\bm{k}}\alpha}^{\dagger}\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial\tau}+\varepsilon({\bm{k}})\right)c_{{\bm{k}}\alpha}+\sum_{\bm{k}}f_{1{\bm{k}}\alpha}^{\dagger}\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial\tau}+\varepsilon_{1}({\bm{k}})\right)f_{1{\bm{k}}\alpha} (8.6)
+∫d2𝒓{s|Φ(𝒓)|2+[g+g′(𝒓)]cα†(𝒓)f1​α(𝒓)Φ(𝒓)+H.c.\displaystyle+\int d^{2}{\bm{r}}\Bigl\{s\,|\Phi({\bm{r}})|^{2}+[g+{\color[rgb]{0,0.3906,0}g^{\prime}({\bm{r}})}]\,c_{\alpha}^{\dagger}({\bm{r}})f_{1\alpha}({\bm{r}})\,\Phi({\bm{r}})+\mbox{H.c.}
+K|∇𝒓Φ(𝒓)|2+u|Φ(𝒓)|4+v(𝒓)[cα†(𝒓)cα(𝒓)+f1​α†(𝒓)f1​α(𝒓)]}.\displaystyle+K\,|\nabla_{\bm{r}}\Phi({\bm{r}})|^{2}+u\,|\Phi({\bm{r}})|^{4}+{\color[rgb]{0,0.3906,0}v({\bm{r}})}\left[c_{\alpha}^{\dagger}({\bm{r}})c_{\alpha}({\bm{r}})+f_{1\alpha}^{\dagger}(\bm{r})f_{1\alpha}(\bm{r})\right]\Bigr\}\,.

We are using the convention that quenched random variables (with no dynamics and a fixed, random dependence on 𝒓{\bm{r}}) are colored in green. For the Kondo lattice case, there should also be a U(1) gauge field associated with Eq. (2.5) in the Lagrangian in Eq. (8.6), but we have dropped it as it does not significantly modify the critical behavior [298, 277]. For the single-band case, there is a SU~​(2)×U​(1)\widetilde{\rm SU}(2)\times{\rm U}(1) gauge field [4, 140, 295], as we review in Appendix B (the tilde is to distinguish from the distinct SU(2) gauge field of Sections 3-6); the U(1) gauge field is the local constraint in the 𝑺1{\bm{S}}_{1} layer (as in Eq. (2.5)), and the SU~​(2)\widetilde{\rm SU}(2) gauge field is the singlet projection between the 𝑺1{\bm{S}}_{1} and 𝑺2{\bm{S}}_{2} layers, and we ignore these gauge fields for similar reasons. The dispersions ε⁡(𝒌)\varepsilon({\bm{k}}) and ε1​(𝒌)\varepsilon_{1}({\bm{k}}) arise from the t𝒊​𝒋t_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}} and t1​𝒊​𝒋t_{1{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}} in Eq. (2.4), ss is the tuning parameter in Fig. 37, and we have added various in an effective action for Φ\Phi.

The most common form of spatial disorder in studies of metallic transport is a random potential from impurities, and this realized by v⁡(𝒓)v({\bm{r}}). This spatial disorder is averaged over after assuming it is uncorrelated at different points in space

v⁡(𝒓)¯=0,v⁡(𝒓)​v​(𝒓′)¯=v2​δ​(𝒓−𝒓′).\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0,0.3906,0}\overline{v({\bm{r}})}=0\quad,\quad\overline{v({\bm{r}})v({\bm{r}^{\prime}})}=v^{2}\delta({\bm{r}}-{\bm{r}^{\prime}})\,.} (8.7)

One of the main new points made in Refs. [298, 139], as we will see in Section 8.2, is that random potential disorder is also not sufficient to produce a strange metal, and the effects of spatial randomness in the interactions [277] must also be considered. Spatial disorder in the Kondo exchange interaction JKJ_{K} in Eq. (2.1) translates into the spatially random Yukawa coupling g′​(𝒓)g^{\prime}({\bm{r}}) which we take to obey the disorder average

g′​(𝒓)¯=0,g′​(𝒓)​g′​(𝒓′)¯=g′2​δ​(𝒓−𝒓′).\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0,0.3906,0}\overline{g^{\prime}({\bm{r}})}=0\quad,\quad\overline{g^{\prime}({\bm{r}})g^{\prime}({\bm{r}^{\prime}})}=g^{\prime 2}\delta({\bm{r}}-{\bm{r}^{\prime}}).} (8.8)

In the underlying electronic model, the exchange JK∼t2/UJ_{K}\sim t^{2}/U, where tt is some hopping–so randomness in tt (which is a form of random potential disorder) translates to randomness in JKJ_{K}, and hence in the Yukawa coupling. We can also see that upon integrating out the fermions, the coupling g′​(𝒓)g^{\prime}({\bm{r}}) generates spatial randomness in ss. The latter is usually identified as ‘Harris disorder’, associated with spatial randomness in the position of the phase transition. But as long as we are in a self-averaging regime, the lesson from the Yukawa-SYK model is that it is more convenient to keep the randomness in the Yukawa coupling. Moreover, we can transfer random mass disorder to random Yukawa coupling disorder simply by rescaling Φ⁡(𝒓)\Phi({\bm{r}}) with a 𝒓{\bm{r}}-dependent factor: so keeping it in g′​(𝒓)g^{\prime}({\bm{r}}) is equivalent to working in the boson eigenstates of the random mass term. At very low energies, the random mass does eventually lead to boson localization and the new physics [177, 178, 138] of the ‘foot’, and this is discussed in Section 9.

The properties of this strange metal theory will be determined by directly extending the methods used to solve the Yukawa-SYK model. This extension can be viewed as simply solving the equations in Fig. 35, while using the propagators in ℒΦ\mathcal{L}_{\Phi}. Alternatively, a fictitious flavor index on all fields ranging over NN values can be introduced and the large NN limit taken, assuming couplings are random in this flavor space. For simplicity, we ignore the difference in dispersion between the cc and f1f_{1} fermions in the remaining discussion: this does not significantly modify the results as long as there is random spatial potential acting on the fermions. Then we obtain a GG-Σ\Sigma-DD-Π\Pi theory which is a direct generalization of Eq. (7.16) to Green’s functions that are bilocal in both space and time

𝒵=∫𝒟​G​𝒟​Σ​𝒟​D​𝒟​Π​exp⁡(−N​Sall)\displaystyle\mathcal{Z}=\int\mathcal{D}G\,\mathcal{D}\Sigma\,\mathcal{D}D\,\mathcal{D}\Pi\exp(-NS_{\rm all})
Sall=−lndet(∂τ+ε(𝒌)−μ+Σ)+12lndet(−∂τ2+𝒒2+mb2−Π)\displaystyle S_{\rm all}=-\ln\det(\partial_{\tau}+\varepsilon({{\bm{k}}})-\mu+\Sigma)+\frac{1}{2}\ln\det(-\partial_{\tau}^{2}+{{\bm{q}}}^{2}+m_{b}^{2}-\Pi)
+∫dτd2r∫dτ′d2r′[−Σ(τ′,𝒓′;τ,𝒓)G(τ,𝒓;τ′,𝒓′)+\displaystyle+\int d\tau d^{2}r\int d\tau^{\prime}d^{2}r^{\prime}\left[-\Sigma(\tau^{\prime},{\bm{r}}^{\prime};\tau,{\bm{r}})G(\tau,{\bm{r}};\tau^{\prime},{\bm{r}}^{\prime})+\right.
12​Π​(τ′,𝒓′,τ,𝒓)​D​(τ,𝒓,τ′,𝒓′)+g22​G​(τ,𝒓,τ′,𝒓′)​G​(τ′,𝒓′,τ,𝒓)​D​(τ,𝒓,τ′,𝒓′)\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\Pi(\tau^{\prime},{\bm{r}}^{\prime};\tau,{\bm{r}})D(\tau,{\bm{r}};\tau^{\prime},{\bm{r}}^{\prime})+\frac{g^{2}}{2}G(\tau,{\bm{r}};\tau^{\prime},{\bm{r}}^{\prime})G(\tau^{\prime},{\bm{r}}^{\prime};\tau,{\bm{r}})D(\tau,{\bm{r}};\tau^{\prime},{\bm{r}}^{\prime})
+v22​G​(τ,𝒓,τ′,𝒓′)​G​(τ′,𝒓′,τ,𝒓)​δ​(𝒓−𝒓′)\displaystyle+\frac{{\color[rgb]{0,0.3906,0}v^{2}}}{2}G(\tau,{\bm{r}};\tau^{\prime},{\bm{r}}^{\prime})G(\tau^{\prime},{\bm{r}}^{\prime};\tau,{\bm{r}})\delta({\bm{r}}-{\bm{r}}^{\prime})
+g′22G(τ,𝒓;τ′,𝒓′)G(τ′,𝒓′;τ,𝒓)D(τ,𝒓;τ′,𝒓′)δ(𝒓−𝒓′)].\displaystyle+\left.\frac{{\color[rgb]{0,0.3906,0}g^{\prime 2}}}{2}G(\tau,{\bm{r}};\tau^{\prime},{\bm{r}}^{\prime})G(\tau^{\prime},{\bm{r}}^{\prime};\tau,{\bm{r}})D(\tau,{\bm{r}};\tau^{\prime},{\bm{r}}^{\prime})\delta({\bm{r}}-{\bm{r}}^{\prime})\right]\,. (8.9)

For compactness of notation and analysis, we have assumed that the cc and f1f_{1} fermions Green’s functions are both equal to GG, but it is not difficult to treat the more general case. Note that the spatially random couplings lead to an additional δ⁡(𝒓−𝒓′)\delta({\bm{r}}-{\bm{r}}^{\prime}) in their contributions arising from the disorder averages in Eqs. (8.7) and (8.8). The saddle point of Eq. (8.9) leads to equations for the Green’s functions which can also be derived from Fig. 35:

Σ⁡(τ,𝒓)=g2​D​(τ,𝒓)​G​(τ,𝒓)+v2​G​(τ,𝒓)​δ2​(𝒓)+g′2​G​(τ,𝒓)​D​(τ,𝒓)​δ2​(𝒓),\displaystyle\Sigma(\tau,{\bm{r}})=g^{2}D(\tau,{\bm{r}})G(\tau,{\bm{r}})+{\color[rgb]{0,0.3906,0}v^{2}}G(\tau,{\bm{r}})\delta^{2}({\bm{r}})+{\color[rgb]{0,0.3906,0}{g^{\prime}}^{2}}G(\tau,{\bm{r}})D(\tau,{\bm{r}})\delta^{2}({\bm{r}}),
Π⁡(τ,𝒓)=−g2​G​(−τ,−𝒓)​G​(τ,𝒓)−g′2​G​(−τ,𝒓)​G​(τ,𝒓)​δ2​(𝒓),\displaystyle\Pi(\tau,{\bm{r}})=-g^{2}G(-\tau,-{\bm{r}})G(\tau,{\bm{r}})-{\color[rgb]{0,0.3906,0}{g^{\prime}}^{2}}G(-\tau,{\bm{r}})G(\tau,{\bm{r}})\delta^{2}({\bm{r}}),
