We also need an equation to determine the boson mass mbm_{b}: this is determined by the Hartree contribution from the uu term in Eq. (8.6) [299].

This is a good point to note the importance of the elastic scattering term v⁡(𝒓)v({\bm{r}}). This broadens the Fermi surfaces, and so effects from Fermi surface nesting or ‘hotspots’ are quenched. This is a key reason for the universality of 𝑳Φ{\bm{L}}_{\Phi}, which applies to symmetry breaking transitions too, along with the non-symmetry breaking FL*-FL transition we are considering. This is also the reason the difference in dispersion between cc and f1f_{1} is mostly not important, and has been neglected above. However, the particle-hole asymmetry of the FL*-FL transition is important for the thermopower, and we comment on this near Eq. (8.14).

Before discussing the solution of Eq. (8.10), the computation of response functions of fermion bilinears, such as the conductivity, is described. These can be obtained by inserting external sources into Eq. (8.9) and then taking the variational derivatives with respect to them. This leads to the graphs shown in Fig. 38, which have to evaluated with fully renormalized Green’s functions.

The following subsections discuss the solutions of the equations in Eq. (8.10) and Fig. 38 for the cases without and with spatial randomness.

8.2 No spatial randomness

The solution of Eq. (8.10) with g≠0g\neq 0, but g′=0g^{\prime}=0 and v=0v=0, is considered. This corresponds to the quantum phase transition without disorder, and has been much studied in the literature. At the quantum critical point, Eq. (8.10) yields a non-Fermi liquid form for the fermion Green’s function, and a Landau-damped form for the boson Green’s function [300, 299]

Σ⁡(i​ω,𝒌)∼−i​sgn​(ω)​|ω|2/3,\displaystyle\Sigma(i\omega,{\bm{k}})\sim-i\mbox{sgn}(\omega)|\omega|^{2/3}\,, G⁡(i​ω,𝒌)=1i​ω−ε⁡(𝒌)−Σ⁡(i​ω,𝒌)\displaystyle\quad G(i\omega,{\bm{k}})=\frac{1}{i\omega-\varepsilon({\bm{k}})-\Sigma(i\omega,{\bm{k}})}
D⁡(i​Ω,𝒒)\displaystyle\quad D(i\Omega,{\bm{q}}) =1Ω2+𝒒2+γ​|Ω|/q,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\Omega^{2}+{\bm{q}}^{2}+\gamma|\Omega|/q}\,, (8.11)

The fermion Green’s function has a sharp Fermi surface in momentum space, and 𝒌{\bm{k}} in Eq. (8.11) is assumed to be close to the Fermi surface. But GG is diffusive in frequency space, indicating the absence of well-defined fermionic quasiparticles.

However, an important point is that essentially none of this non-Fermi liquid structure feeds into the conductivity, which remains very similar to that of a Fermi liquid [301, 302, 303, 144, 298, 304, 305] with the form:

σ⁡(ω)∼1−i​ω+|ω|0+⋯(ω−2/3 term has vanishing co-efficient)\displaystyle\sigma(\omega)\sim\frac{1}{-i\omega}+|\omega|^{0}+\cdots\quad\mbox{($\omega^{-2/3}$ term has vanishing co-efficient)} (8.12)

There has been a claim [306] of a ω−2/3\omega^{-2/3} contribution to the conductivity, but its co-efficient vanishes after evaluation of all the graphs in Fig. 38 [304, 298]. This cancellation can be understood as a consequence of Kohn’s theorem [307], which states that in a Galilean-invariant system only the first term of the right-hand-side of Eq. (8.12) is non-zero. A Galilean-invariant system is not considered here, but all contributions to the possible ω−2/3\omega^{-2/3} term arise from long-wavelength processes in the vicinity of patches of the Fermi surface, and these patches can be embedded in a system which is Galilean-invariant also at higher energies.

8.3 With spatial randomness

The absence of the ω−2/3\omega^{-2/3} term in Eq. (8.12) is a strong indication that the resolution of the strange metal problem cannot come from the clean limit of quantum-critical theories described by models of the class in Eq. (8.6). There can be umklapp processes which dissipate momentum, but these require special features of the Fermi surface to survive at low momentum. Recent nonlinear THz 2D coherent spectroscopy observations on the cuprates [308] observe a rapid momentum relaxation rate, supporting models in which disorder plays a central role.

A theory with only potential scattering disorder as in Eq. (8.7), i.e. g≠0g\neq 0, v≠0v\neq 0, but g′=0g^{\prime}=0, is also not sufficient [298, 309]: it leads to marginal Fermi-liquid behavior in the electron self energy, but no strange metal behavior in transport. So for a generic and universal theory of strange metals, the influence of disorder with gg, g′g^{\prime}, and vv all non-zero should be considered. The solution of Eq. (8.10) yields a boson Green’s function which has a diffusive form at the critical point [310]

D⁡(i​Ω,𝒒)∼1𝒒2+γ​|Ω|.\displaystyle D(i\Omega,{\bm{q}})\sim\frac{1}{{\bm{q}}^{2}+\gamma|\Omega|}\,. (8.13)

This is a good point to mention, in passing, a special feature of the FL*-FL transition, not shared by phase transitions of two-dimensional metals with symmetry breaking order parameters. The Φ\Phi propagator of the FL*-FL transition is sensitive to particle-hole asymmetry, as it also carries electrical charge (for ℒΦ\mathcal{L}_{\Phi}, the asymmetry requires ε⁡(𝒌)≠ε1​(𝒌)\varepsilon({\bm{k}})\neq\varepsilon_{1}({\bm{k}})). This allows a more general form for the boson propagator than Eq. (8.13) [277, 171]

D⁡(i​Ω,𝒒)∼1𝒒2+γ​|Ω|−i​γ¯​Ω.D(i\Omega,{\bm{q}})\sim\frac{1}{{\bm{q}}^{2}+\gamma|\Omega|-i\bar{\gamma}\Omega}\,. (8.14)

The γ¯\bar{\gamma} term is responsible for the singular thermopower response, as discussed in Ref. [171], and this connects to observations on Fermi volume changing transitions in cuprates [172, 173, 174] and heavy-fermion compounds [175].

Inserting Eq. (8.13) or (8.14) into the fermion Green’s function gives a marginal Fermi liquid form [310, 139]

G⁡(ω)∼1ω​m∗​(ω)m−ε⁡(𝒌)+i⁡(1τe+1τin​(ω))​sgn​(ω)\displaystyle G(\omega)\sim\frac{1}{\displaystyle\omega\,\frac{m^{\ast}(\omega)}{m}-\varepsilon({\bm{k}})+i\left(\frac{1}{\tau_{e}}+\frac{1}{\tau_{\rm in}(\omega)}\right)\mbox{sgn}(\omega)} (8.15)
1τe∼v2;1τin​(ω)∼(g2v2+g′2)​|ω|;m∗​(ω)m∼2π​(g2v2+g′2)​ln⁡(Λ/ω).\displaystyle\frac{1}{\tau_{e}}\sim{\color[rgb]{0,0.3906,0}v^{2}}\,;\quad\frac{1}{\tau_{\rm in}(\omega)}\sim\left(\frac{g^{2}}{{\color[rgb]{0,0.3906,0}v^{2}}}+{\color[rgb]{0,0.3906,0}g^{\prime 2}}\right)|\omega|\,;\quad\frac{m^{\ast}(\omega)}{m}\sim\frac{2}{\pi}\left(\frac{g^{2}}{{\color[rgb]{0,0.3906,0}v^{2}}}+{\color[rgb]{0,0.3906,0}g^{\prime 2}}\right)\ln(\Lambda/\omega)\,.

The expressions in the second line are schematic, and show only the dependence upon gg, g′g^{\prime} and vv without numerical constants. This result matches the photoemission observations in Eq. (8.3) for α=1/2\alpha=1/2. Note that there are two distinct contributions to the singular |ω||\omega| electron inelastic scattering rate 1/τin1/\tau_{\rm in}: one from the combination of impurity scattering vv with the spatially uniform interaction gg [310], and the other from the spatially random interaction g′g^{\prime} [277, 139].

Inserting these solutions for the Green’s functions into the action in Eq. (8.9), gives a T​ln⁡(1/T)T\ln(1/T) specific heat [299].

Turning to the evaluation of the conductivity graphs in Fig. 38, the key property of the strange metal, the conductivity, is given by the form in Eq. (8.2), with [277, 139]

1τtrans​(ω)∼v2\displaystyle\frac{1}{\tau_{\rm trans}(\omega)}\sim{\color[rgb]{0,0.3906,0}v^{2}} +g′2​|ω|;mtrans∗​(ω)m∼2​g′2π​ln⁡(Λ/ω)\displaystyle+{\color[rgb]{0,0.3906,0}g^{\prime 2}}|\omega|\quad;\quad\frac{m_{\rm trans}^{\ast}(\omega)}{m}\sim\frac{2{\color[rgb]{0,0.3906,0}g^{\prime 2}}}{\pi}\ln(\Lambda/\omega) (8.16)

This expression shows that the residual resistivity ρ0\rho_{0} at T=0T=0 is determined by the elastic scattering rate 1/τe∼v21/\tau_{e}\sim{\color[rgb]{0,0.3906,0}v^{2}}, as in a disordered Fermi liquid. The inelastic processes lead to a frequency and temperature dependence which matches precisely with the observational form in Eq. (8.2). An important feature is that of the two processes contributing to the electron inelastic scattering rate 1/τin1/\tau_{\rm in} in Eq. (8.15), only one contributes to the inelastic transport rate 1/τtrans1/\tau_{\rm trans}. The processes involving the spatially uniform interaction gg and the impurity potential vv cancel out in the computation of the conductivity from Fig. 38, and only those involving the spatially random interaction g′g^{\prime} survive [139]. A consequence of this cancellation is that the constant α~\widetilde{\alpha} in Eq. (8.5) approaches α~=π/2\widetilde{\alpha}=\pi/2 for the quasiparticle m∗m^{\ast} in the limit g′≫g{\color[rgb]{0,0.3906,0}g^{\prime}}\gg g [299], and decreases from this value as gg is increased [139].

To summarize, the conductivity of the theory ℒΦ\mathcal{L}_{\Phi} yields the strange metal conductivity in Eq. (8.1), with ρ0∼v2\rho_{0}\sim{\color[rgb]{0,0.3906,0}v^{2}} and A∼g′2A\sim{\color[rgb]{0,0.3906,0}g^{\prime 2}}. Note that the value of gg does not make a direct difference to the value of the linear-TT resistivity, although it does affect the marginal Fermi liquid behavior of the electron self energy, as noted in Eq. (8.15). It is also notable that the residual resistivity and linear-TT resistivity slope are determined by different sources of disorder: those in Eqs. (8.7) and (8.8) respectively. This distinction should be important in understanding trends in observations [311, 312]. In the quantum critical region, the approach outlined above [139], and the more complete quantum Monte Carlo studies [178] show that the slope α~\widetilde{\alpha} of the transport scattering rate in Eq. (8.5) is largely independent of the strength of disorder.

We note that a full numerical solution of Eq. (8.10) at g=0g=0 has been presented by Li et al. [169], including results for the conductivity and the onset of superconductivity. Their results for the transport scattering time τtrans\tau_{\rm trans} are shown in Fig. 39, along with the corresponding optical conductivity observations of Michon et al [286]. Both obey the Planckian scaling form in Eq. (8.2) reasonably well. The scaling is better in the experimental observations, and we suspect this is the due to the logarithmic violations in the theory, such as those in Eq. (8.16). It would be interesting to extend the study of optical conductivity to the quantum Monte Carlo approach [178] in future work.

The key role of spatial randomness in the Yukawa coupling in this theory implies a prediction: correlated electron systems will not exhibit low TT strange metal behavior in sufficiently clean samples. Evidence in support of this prediction has appeared in recent experiments on graphene: while twisted bilayer graphene has a strange metal phase [313], the much cleaner system of rhombohedral trilayer graphene does not [314].

Finally, note that a recent computation [315] of shot noise in the g′g^{\prime}-vv model yields results in agreement with observations [316]. The g′g^{\prime}-vv model has also been used to study non-linear optical response [317], and there are interesting connections to recent observations [308]

9 Boson localization and Griffiths phase

This section turns to the behavior of the optimally and overdoped cuprates at low temperatures. When the superconductivity is suppressed by a strong magnetic field, the transport properties show an extended regime of non-Fermi liquid behavior, commonly associated with the ‘foot’ in the phase diagram of Ref. [179], and also observed in Refs. [180, 182, 181].

We address this behavior by examining non-self-averaging features of the model of Section 8. At lower TT, we expect a crossover from the fractionalized degrees of freedom to confinement: so we will replace the Higgs boson Φ\Phi by a spin density wave (SDW) order parameter [138], and consider the disordered version of the transition at psdwp_{\rm sdw} in Fig. 1.

We write the spin density wave order as (a=x,y,za=x,y,z)

Sa​(𝒓)=∑ℓϕℓ​a​ei​𝑸ℓ⋅𝒓S_{a}({\bm{r}})=\sum_{\ell}\phi_{\ell a}e^{i{\bm{Q}}_{\ell}\cdot{\bm{r}}} (9.1)

where ℓ=1​…​4\ell=1\dots 4 labels the 4 ordering wavevectors 𝑸ℓ{\bm{Q}}_{\ell} at (π⁡(1±δ),π)(\pi(1\pm\delta),\pi) and (π,π⁡(1±δ))(\pi,\pi(1\pm\delta)). We are interested in fluctuations of the SDW order parameters ϕℓ​a\phi_{\ell a} coupled to electrons c𝒌​σc_{{\bm{k}}\sigma} with dispersion ε⁡(𝒌)\varepsilon({\bm{k}}) which has a Fermi surface. We describe this with a 2D-YSYK model [299, 139] with imaginary time (τ\tau) Lagrangian (replacing ℒΦ\mathcal{L}_{\Phi} in Eq. (8.6))

ℒϕ\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\phi} =∑𝒌c𝒌​α†(∂∂τ+ε(𝒌))c𝒌​α+∫d2𝒓{s[ϕ(𝒓)]2\displaystyle=\sum_{{\bm{k}}}c_{{\bm{k}}\alpha}^{\dagger}\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial\tau}+\varepsilon({\bm{k}})\right)c_{{\bm{k}}\alpha}+\int d^{2}{\bm{r}}\,\Bigl\{s\,[\phi({\bm{r}})]^{2} (9.2)
+∑ℓ[g+g′(𝒓)]cα†(𝒓)σα​βacβ(𝒓)ϕℓ​a(𝒓)ei​𝑸ℓ⋅𝒓+K[∇𝒓ϕ(𝒓)]2+u[ϕ(𝒓)]4\displaystyle+\sum_{\ell}[g+{\color[rgb]{0,0.3906,0}g^{\prime}({\bm{r}})}]c^{\dagger}_{\alpha}({\bm{r}})\sigma^{a}_{\alpha\beta}c_{\beta}({\bm{r}})\,\phi_{\ell a}({\bm{r}})e^{i{\bm{Q}}_{\ell}\cdot{\bm{r}}}+K\,[\nabla_{\bm{r}}\phi({\bm{r}})]^{2}+u\,[\phi({\bm{r}})]^{4}
+v(𝒓)cα†(𝒓)cα(𝒓)}.\displaystyle~~~~~~~~~+{\color[rgb]{0,0.3906,0}v({\bm{r}})}c_{\alpha}^{\dagger}({\bm{r}})c_{\alpha}({\bm{r}})\Bigr\}\,.

The self-averaging behavior of this theory is essentially the same as that of ℒΦ\mathcal{L}_{\Phi} in Eq. (8.6), leading to equations closely related to those in Eq. (8.10). We will instead examine the low TT physics here, where there is a breakdown of self-averaging, and the local environment near each impurity can behave differently.

The dominant effect associated with breakdown of self-averaging in disordered metals is the localization of the electronic quasiparticle eigenstates. This will also be present in the theory in Eq. (9.2), associated with the random potential v⁡(𝒓)v({\bm{r}}). However, in d=2d=2, such electron localization effects are only marginally relevant at weak disorder [318]. In contrast, the effects due to the random interaction g′​(𝒓)g^{\prime}({\bm{r}}) are significantly stronger [319, 320, 321]. The latter effects are associated with local shifts in the deviation from criticality, and their relevance is determined by the Harris criterion [322, 323]: the exponent of critical point shifts is 2/ν−d2/\nu-d. The disorder free theory has ν=1/2\nu=1/2, implying a strong violation of the Harris criterion, and strong relevance of the disorder associated with g′​(𝒓)g^{\prime}({\bm{r}})—we will focus on this disorder in the remainder of this section. We note that a focus on bosonic disorder and localization is also a feature of works postulating two-level systems [324, 325, 326].

9.1 Strong disorder renormalization group

Given the strong relevance of weak g′g^{\prime}, it is natural to examine the limit of strong disorder. This was examined in Refs. [176, 327, 328]. They proceeded by integrating out the fermions, assuming the fermions remain extended over the relevant energy scales. This leads to the following effective action for the boson ϕ\phi:

𝒮\displaystyle\mathcal{S} =\displaystyle= 𝒮K​ϕ+𝒮ϕ​d\displaystyle\mathcal{S}_{K\phi}+\mathcal{S}_{\phi d}
𝒮K​ϕ\displaystyle\mathcal{S}_{K\phi} =\displaystyle= ∫dτ[−∑𝒊<𝒋K𝒊​𝒋ϕ𝒊​aϕ𝒋​a+∑𝒋{s𝒋2ϕ𝒋​a2+u4​M(ϕ𝒋​a2)2}]\displaystyle\int d\tau\Biggl[-\sum_{{\bm{i}}<{\bm{j}}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.3906,0}K_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}}\phi_{{\bm{i}}a}\phi_{{\bm{j}}a}+\sum_{{\bm{j}}}\biggl\{\frac{{\color[rgb]{0,0.3906,0}s_{{\bm{j}}}}}{2}\phi_{{\bm{j}}a}^{2}+\frac{u}{4M}\left(\phi_{{\bm{j}}a}^{2}\right)^{2}\biggr\}\Biggr]
𝒮ϕ​d\displaystyle\mathcal{S}_{\phi d} =\displaystyle= T2​∑Ω∑𝒋(γ​|Ω|+Ω2/c2)​|ϕ𝒋​a​(i​Ω)|2,\displaystyle\frac{T}{2}\sum_{\Omega}\sum_{\bm{j}}\left(\gamma|\Omega|+\Omega^{2}/c^{2}\right)|\phi_{{\bm{j}}a}(i\Omega)|^{2}\,, (9.3)

We have combined the indices ℓ,a\ell,a in Eq. (9.1) into a single index a=1​…​Ma=1\ldots M, with M=12M=12 the case of interest. The Landau damping from the fermions is represented by 𝒮ϕ​d\mathcal{S}_{\phi d}, and the disorder in g′​(𝒓)g^{\prime}({\bm{r}}) has led to the disordered couplings K𝒊​𝒋K_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}} and s𝒋s_{\bm{j}} in 𝒮K​ϕ\mathcal{S}_{K\phi}. The Dasgupta-Ma [329] strong disorder renormalization group of proceeds by identifying the sites with the largest values of K𝒊​𝒋K_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}} or s𝒊s_{\bm{i}}, and integrates out the fluctuations of corresponding ϕ𝒊\phi_{\bm{i}}—the details of the computation are presented in Ref. [327]. If the largest coupling is s2s_{2}, then we can integrate out the fluctuations of ϕ2\phi_{2}, and the remaining couplings renormalize as

K~𝒊​𝒋=K𝒊​𝒋+K𝒊​2​K2​𝒋s2,𝒊,𝒋≠2.{\color[rgb]{0,0.3906,0}\widetilde{K}_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}}={\color[rgb]{0,0.3906,0}K_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}}+{\color[rgb]{0,0.3906,0}\frac{K_{{\bm{i}}2}K_{2{\bm{j}}}}{s_{2}}}\quad,\quad{\bm{i}},{\bm{j}}\neq 2\,. (9.4)

If the largest coupling is K23K_{23} then we replace ϕ2\phi_{2} and ϕ3\phi_{3} with a single boson ϕ~2\widetilde{\phi}_{2} with renormalized couplings

s~2=2​s2​s3K23,K~2​𝒋=K2​𝒋+K3​𝒋,𝒋≠2,3.{\color[rgb]{0,0.3906,0}\widetilde{s}_{2}}=2{\color[rgb]{0,0.3906,0}\frac{s_{2}s_{3}}{K_{23}}}\quad,\quad{\color[rgb]{0,0.3906,0}\widetilde{K}_{2{\bm{j}}}}={\color[rgb]{0,0.3906,0}K_{2{\bm{j}}}}+{\color[rgb]{0,0.3906,0}K_{3{\bm{j}}}}\quad,\quad{\bm{j}}\neq 2,3\,. (9.5)

Remarkably, these are the same renormalization group equations as those for the quantum Ising model with random exchange and transverse field [176, 327, 328]

HRIM=−∑𝒊<𝒋K𝒊​𝒋Z𝒊Z𝒋−∑𝒊s𝒊X𝒊,H_{\rm RIM}=-\sum_{{\bm{i}}<{\bm{j}}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.3906,0}K_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}}Z_{\bm{i}}Z_{\bm{j}}-\sum_{{\bm{i}}}{\color[rgb]{0,0.3906,0}s_{\bm{i}}}X_{\bm{i}}\,, (9.6)

where X𝒊X_{\bm{i}}, Z𝒊Z_{\bm{i}} are Pauli operators on qubits on sites 𝒊{\bm{i}}. The solutions of renormalization group equations of this model in two spatial dimensions have been studied numerically in Ref. [330]—they found a critical point controlled by an infinite randomness fixed point, along with Griffiths phase with continuously varying exponents on the disordered side.

This mapping between theories in Eqs. (9.3) and (9.6) does appear rather surprising. The former has a multicomponent order parameter with a continuous symmetry which is Landau-damped, whereas the latter has a discrete symmetry and no Landau-damping. But the connection between them can be seen by examining the rare-region arguments in Refs. [331, 332]. Consider a rare region of size LL in which is deep within the ordered phase. This will occur with a probability ∼exp⁡(−c1​Ld)\sim\exp(-c_{1}L^{d}), and have an effective moment of size LdL^{d}. Considering the temporal fluctuations of this block spin for the Ising case as a one-dimensional classical Ising model, we obtain a correlation time of order ξτ∼exp⁡(c2​Ld)\xi_{\tau}\sim\exp(c_{2}L^{d}). Correspondingly, for the continuous symmetry case, the Landau-damping implies a 1/|τ|21/|\tau|^{2} temporal interaction for the block spin, and this also has a correlation time of order ξτ∼exp⁡(c¯2​Ld)\xi_{\tau}\sim\exp(\bar{c}_{2}L^{d}) [333]. Adding the contribution of these rare regions by the saddle-point method, we obtain a power-law Griffiths singularity in the local density of states [331, 332] in both cases.

9.2 Large MM theory

While the mapping to the quantum Ising model yields considerable insight on the strong disorder limit, our interest is also in systems with weak disorder, and of the crossover to the self-averaging physics studied in Section 8. To this end, we follow the large MM analysis of Refs. [334, 177]. For convenience, we retain disorder only in the random ‘mass’ term, as that will generate disorder in other couplings; so we replace 𝒮K​ϕ\mathcal{S}_{K\phi} in Eq. (9.3) by

𝒮ϕ=∫d​τ​[K2​∑⟨𝒊​𝒋⟩(ϕ𝒊​a−ϕ𝒋​a)2+∑𝒋{s+δ​s𝒋2​ϕ𝒋​a2+u4​M​(ϕ𝒋​a2)2}].\mathcal{S}_{\phi}=\int d\tau\Biggl[\frac{K}{2}\sum_{\langle{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}\rangle}\left(\phi_{{\bm{i}}a}-\phi_{{\bm{j}}a}\right)^{2}+\sum_{{\bm{j}}}\biggl\{\frac{s+{\color[rgb]{0,0.3906,0}\delta s_{{\bm{j}}}}}{2}\phi_{{\bm{j}}a}^{2}+\frac{u}{4M}\left(\phi_{{\bm{j}}a}^{2}\right)^{2}\biggr\}\Biggr]\,. (9.7)

Then the large MM saddle point equations are

𝒮~ϕ=\displaystyle\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}_{\phi}= ∫d​τ​[K2​∑⟨𝒊​𝒋⟩(ϕ𝒊​a−ϕ𝒋​a)2+∑js~𝒋2​ϕ𝒋​a2]\displaystyle\int d\tau\Bigl[\frac{K}{2}\sum_{\langle{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}\rangle}\left(\phi_{{\bm{i}}a}-\phi_{{\bm{j}}a}\right)^{2}+\sum_{j}\frac{{\color[rgb]{0,0.3906,0}\widetilde{s}_{\bm{j}}}}{2}\phi_{{\bm{j}}a}^{2}\Bigr] (9.8)
s~𝒋=s+δ​s𝒋+uM​∑a⟨ϕ𝒋​a2⟩𝒮~ϕ+𝒮ϕ​d\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0,0.3906,0}\widetilde{s}_{\bm{j}}}=s+{\color[rgb]{0,0.3906,0}\delta s_{\bm{j}}}+\frac{u}{M}\sum_{a}\left\langle\phi_{{\bm{j}}a}^{2}\right\rangle_{\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}_{\phi}+\mathcal{S}_{\phi d}}
=s+δ​s𝒋+u​T​∑Ω∑αψα​𝒊​ψα​𝒋γ​|Ω|+Ω2/c2+eα,\displaystyle~~~=s+{\color[rgb]{0,0.3906,0}\delta s_{\bm{j}}}+uT\sum_{\Omega}\sum_{\alpha}\frac{\psi_{\alpha{\bm{i}}}\psi_{\alpha{\bm{j}}}}{\gamma|\Omega|+\Omega^{2}/c^{2}+e_{\alpha}}\,,

where eαe_{\alpha} and ψα​𝒋\psi_{\alpha{\bm{j}}} are eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of the ϕ\phi quadratic form in 𝒮~ϕ\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}_{\phi}, labeled by the index α=1​…​L2\alpha=1\ldots L^{2} for a L×LL\times L sample. For each disorder realization δ​sj\delta s_{j}, the values of s~j\color[rgb]{0,0.3906,0}\widetilde{s}_{j} are determined by numerically solving (9.8), and this also yields results for the eigenvalues eαe_{\alpha} and the eigenvectors ψα​j\psi_{\alpha j}.

Numerical results obtained from the solution of Eq. (9.8) at the quantum critical value s=scs=s_{c} appear in Fig. 40. We show the localization length ℒα\mathcal{L}_{\alpha} of the eigenmodes at energy eαe_{\alpha}. At large eαe_{\alpha}, the value of ℒα\mathcal{L}_{\alpha} is of order the system size, implying extended bosonic eigenmodes, and the applicability of the self-averaging 2D-YSYK theory of Section 8. As we lower eαe_{\alpha}, there is a minimum in eαe_{\alpha}, associated with localization of the bosonic eigenmodes. Below the minimum, we find a logarithmic increase of ℒα\mathcal{L}_{\alpha} with decreasing eαe_{\alpha}: this logarithmic increase is precisely that expected from the infinite-randomness fixed point of the Ising model in a transverse field [184] in Eq. (9.6).

9.3 Quantum Monte Carlo

Ref. [178] examined the complete original model of interacting bosons and fermions in Eq. (9.2) by quantum Monte Carlo simulations. They employed a fermion dispersion to allow a sign-problem-free study [335], and set the average Yukawa coupling to g=0g=0. The determined the bosonic eigenmodes by digaonalizing the zero frequency susceptibility matrix for each realization of the disorder

χ𝒊​𝒋​(i​Ω=0)=∫01/Td​τ​⟨ϕ𝒊​a​(τ)​ϕ𝒋​(0)⟩.\chi_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}(i\Omega=0)=\int_{0}^{1/T}d\tau\left\langle\phi_{{\bm{i}}a}(\tau)\phi_{\bm{j}}(0)\right\rangle\,. (9.9)

Their results for the boson localization length are very similar to those of the large MM computation in Fig. 40. We show instead the Monte Carlo results for the averaged energy of the lowest boson eigenmode e¯0\overline{e}_{0} in Fig. 41. The results show a low temperature ‘foot’ of very small gaps, which we interpret as the analog of the Griffiths phase of the quantum Ising model [184].

9.4 Neutron scattering

Neutron scattering experiments on La2-xSrxCuO4 have observed critical spin fluctuations at a wide range of dopings [336, 181]. Fig. 42a,b show good ‘Planckian’ scaling fits of the dynamic scaling of the suspectibility at the ordering wavevectors 𝑸ℓ{\bm{Q}}_{\ell} at doping x=0.22x=0.22

χ′′​(ω)∼T−α​Φχ​(ℏ​ωkB​T).\chi^{\prime\prime}(\omega)\sim T^{-\alpha}\Phi_{\chi}\left(\frac{\hbar\omega}{k_{B}T}\right)\,. (9.10)

These results have been interpreted [181] in terms of the Griffiths phase of the spin density wave ordering transition. Fig. 42c,d show results obtained by the exact analytic continuation of the numerical solution of the large MM equations in Eq. (9.8), which are also found to obey Planckian scaling to a reasonable accuracy. The data in Fig. 42d are for the quantum critical point, where the value of the exponent α\alpha is larger than the experimental value. However, the large-MM value of α\alpha decreases when we move into the Griffiths phase, as is appropriate for the doping of x=0.22x=0.22. The full Monte Carlo simulation of Eq. (9.2) [178] yields a value of α\alpha close to the experimental observation [181].

9.5 Photoemission

Finally, we turn to the remarkable photoemission data of Reber et al. [182]. From measurements of the electron spectral function along the Brillouin zone diagonals across a wide range of temperatures, frequencies, and dopings in Bi2Sr2CaCu2O8+δ, they argue for a ‘power-law liquid’ across a wide range of dopings. They fit the imaginary part of the electron self energy to the form (corresponding to the scaling form in Eq. (8.3))

Σ′′​(ω)=Γ0+λ​[(ℏ​ω)2+(β​kB​T)2]α(ℏ​ωN)2​α−1,\Sigma^{\prime\prime}(\omega)=\Gamma_{0}+\lambda\frac{[(\hbar\omega)^{2}+(\beta k_{B}T)^{2}]^{\alpha}}{(\hbar\omega_{N})^{2\alpha-1}}\,, (9.11)

and the values of their fit parameters α,λ,β\alpha,\lambda,\beta are shown in Fig. 43a.

The electron self energy and optical conductivity was also computed in the Monte Carlo study of Ref. [178] across the Griffiths phase. The value of their exponent xx of the TT dependence of the relaxation rates is shown in Fig. 43b. This is in reasonable agreement with the expected relation x=2​αx=2\alpha with the experimental data. But note that there is a plateau in the value of xx in the theory, that is (as yet) not visible in the experimental data.

Appendix A. Schrieffer-Wolff transformation from the ALM to the Hubbard model

Here we present an alternative derivation of the connection between the Hubbard model and the ALM, which is also illustrated in Fig. 7. We begin with a Hubbard model and augment it with ancillas which are decoupled from the Hubbard model. It is important that the new degrees of freedom have a trivial ground state with an energy gap, so that its extra excited states can be eliminated by a canonical transformation. For the ancillas, we choose a pair of qubits associated with every site of the square lattice, which we identify as S=1/2S=1/2 spins 𝑺1​𝒊{\bm{S}}_{1{\bm{i}}} and 𝑺2​𝒊{\bm{S}}_{2{\bm{i}}}. There is an antiferromagnetic exchange interaction J⟂J_{\perp} between the two spins at each 𝒊{\bm{i}}, and so the ancillas form a bilayer square lattice antiferromagnet. We take J⟂J_{\perp} to be large enough so that the ground state of the bilayer is smoothly connected to the ‘trivial’ rung singlet state. The decoupled ancilla Hamiltonian is therefore

ℋancilla−decoupled=ℋHubbard+J⟂​∑𝒊𝑺1​𝒊⋅𝑺2​𝒊+…,\mathcal{H}_{\rm ancilla-decoupled}=\mathcal{H}_{\rm Hubbard}+J_{\perp}\sum_{{\bm{i}}}{\bm{S}}_{1{\bm{i}}}\cdot{\bm{S}}_{2{\bm{i}}}+\ldots\,, (.12)

where the ellipses represent exchange interactions within the ancilla layers. As indicated in Fig. 7, we proceed in a direction opposite to that of the paramagnon derivation. Starting from ℋALM\mathcal{H}_{\rm ALM}, we perform a Schrieffer-Wolff transformation to map to ℋancilla−decoupled\mathcal{H}_{\rm ancilla-decoupled} [218]. This Schrieffer-Wolff transformation eliminates all the excited states of the ancilla spins in powers of 1/J⟂1/J_{\perp}, and returns to the single band Hubbard model for the c𝒊​αc_{{\bm{i}}\alpha}, with the value of UU shown below in Eq. (.16) and Fig. 7 [218]. At leading order in 1/J⟂1/J_{\perp}, we can demonstrate this mapping by considering only a single value of 𝒊{\bm{i}}. Then at each 𝒊{\bm{i}}, the ancilla Hamiltonian is

H1=J⟂​𝑺1⋅𝑺2−μ​cα†​cα+JK​𝑺1⋅cα†​𝝈α​β2​cβH_{1}=J_{\perp}{\bm{S}}_{1}\cdot{\bm{S}}_{2}-\mu c_{\alpha}^{\dagger}c_{\alpha}+J_{K}{\bm{S}}_{1}\cdot c_{\alpha}^{\dagger}\frac{{\bm{\sigma}}_{\alpha\beta}}{2}c_{\beta} (.13)

At large J⟂J_{\perp}, the 𝑺1,2{\bm{S}}_{1,2} form a spin singlet, and there are 4 low-lying states of the cαc_{\alpha}. Upon considering perturbation theory in JKJ_{K}, the energies EnE_{n} of the state with nn fermions are

E0\displaystyle E_{0} =\displaystyle= −3​J⟂4,E2=−3​J⟂4−2​μ,\displaystyle-\frac{3J_{\perp}}{4},~~E_{2}=-\frac{3J_{\perp}}{4}-2\mu\,,
E1\displaystyle E_{1} =\displaystyle= −3​J⟂4−μ−3​JK216​J⟂+𝒪⁡(1/J⟂2).\displaystyle-\frac{3J_{\perp}}{4}-\mu-\frac{3J_{K}^{2}}{16J_{\perp}}+\mathcal{O}(1/J_{\perp}^{2})\,. (.14)

These states map onto those of a Hubbard model

H2=−μ′​cα†​cα+U⁡(c↑†​c↑)​(c↓†​c↓)H_{2}=-\mu^{\prime}c_{\alpha}^{\dagger}c_{\alpha}+U(c_{\uparrow}^{\dagger}c_{\uparrow})(c_{\downarrow}^{\dagger}c_{\downarrow}) (.15)

with parameters

U=3​JK28​J⟂,μ′=μ+3​JK216​J⟂.U=\frac{3J_{K}^{2}}{8J_{\perp}},\quad\mu^{\prime}=\mu+\frac{3J_{K}^{2}}{16J_{\perp}}\,. (.16)

Extending this mapping to all sites, we obtain the canonical (Schrieffer-Wolff) transformation connecting ℋALM\mathcal{H}_{\rm ALM} in Eq. (2.10) to ℋancilla−decoupled\mathcal{H}_{\rm ancilla-decoupled} in Eq. (.12).

Appendix B. Complete gauge theory of the ALM

The ancilla representation of the single-band Hubbard model has a SU​(2)×SU~​(2)×U​(1){\rm SU}(2)\times\widetilde{\rm SU}(2)\times{\rm U}(1) gauge structure [4, 140, 7], as we indicated below Eq. (8.6). These 3 gauge fields are connected to three distinct constraints that need to be imposed on the three-layer ALM so that it reduces to the single-layer Hubbard model.

  • •

    The SU(2) gauge field U𝒊​𝒋U_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}} was that introduced in Section 3, and it implements the local constraint Eq. (3.29) in the bottom layer of 𝑺2{\bm{S}}_{2} spins defined by Eq. (5.1).

  • •

    The U(1) gauge field ei​a𝒊​𝒋e^{ia_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}} is that associated with Eq. (2.5) and the constraint Eq. (2.3).

  • •

    While the two gauge fields above have quite familiar origins from on-site constraints, the third SU~​(2)\widetilde{\rm SU}(2) gauge field has a different origin. It is associated with the requirement that the 𝑺1​𝒊{\bm{S}}_{1{\bm{i}}} and 𝑺2​𝒊{\bm{S}}_{2{\bm{i}}} have singlet correlations, and their triplet state should only be a virtual state. This requirement can be implemented by transforming them to a common rotating reference frame in spin space, which introduces a SU~​(2)\widetilde{\rm SU}(2) gauge field [195]; performing the integral over the SU~​(2)\widetilde{\rm SU}(2) gauge field averages over rotating reference frames, and hence projects 𝑺1​𝒊+𝑺2​𝒊{\bm{S}}_{1{\bm{i}}}+{\bm{S}}_{2{\bm{i}}} to the singlet. This SU~​(2)\widetilde{\rm SU}(2) gauge field is closely related to that in other approaches to the pseudogap in the single-band Hubbard model [196, 197, 198, 199, 200, 205, 201, 202, 203, 204]. Sections 3-6 considered a limiting case of the ancilla layer theory, appropriate for the present FL* theory of the pseudogap, where the SU~​(2)\widetilde{\rm SU}(2) gauge field is fully higgsed, and so can be neglected. But the SU~​(2)\widetilde{\rm SU}(2) gauge field is needed for a proper description of the FL state, so that it can confine 𝑺1​𝒊{\bm{S}}_{1{\bm{i}}} and 𝑺2​𝒊{\bm{S}}_{2{\bm{i}}} to rung-singlets in the FL state of Fig. 8 at large doping.

Next, we list the matter content of the ALM.

  • •

    The fermionic electrons c𝒊​αc_{{\bm{i}}\alpha} in the top layer. These are also represented by 𝒞𝒊\mathcal{C}_{\bm{i}} in Eq. (4).

  • •

    The fermionic spinons f1​𝒊​αf_{1{\bm{i}}\alpha} representing the 𝐒1​𝒊{\bf S}_{1{\bm{i}}} spins of the middle layer via Eq. (2.2). These are also represented by ℱ1​𝒊\mathcal{F}_{1{\bm{i}}} defined in Eq. (5.2).

  • •

    The fermionic spinons f𝒊​αf_{{\bm{i}}\alpha} representing the 𝐒2​𝒊{\bf S}_{2{\bm{i}}} spins of the bottom layer via Eq. (5.1). These are also represented by ℱ𝒊\mathcal{F}_{{\bm{i}}} defined in Eq. (3.30).

  • •

    The Higgs boson Φ𝒊​α​β\Phi_{{\bm{i}}\alpha\beta} obtained by decoupling the exchange interaction JKJ_{K} between the top two layers [4]. In Sections 2-6 we assumed this boson was condensed with Φ𝒊​α​β=Φ𝒊​δα​β\Phi_{{\bm{i}}\alpha\beta}=\Phi_{\bm{i}}\delta_{\alpha\beta}. In Section 8, we considered fluctuations of Φ\Phi, but only of its diagonal component for simplicity. This boson is the analog of the ‘slave boson’ which appears in theories of the heavy Fermi liquid state of the Kondo lattice, where it has only a single component.

  • •

    The boson B𝒊B_{\bm{i}} obtained by decoupling the exchange interaction J⟂J_{\perp} between the lower two layers of 𝑺1​𝒊{\bm{S}}_{1{\bm{i}}} and 𝑺2​𝒊{\bm{S}}_{2{\bm{i}}} spins [105]. This is also represented by ℬ𝒊\mathcal{B}_{\bm{i}}, as defined in Eq. (4).

We are now ready to specify gauge and global symmetry transformations of all the fields, which are summarized in Table 3.

Similarly, the global electromagnetic charge transformation of Eq. (4.10) now acts on Φ\Phi:

c𝒊​α\displaystyle c_{{\bm{i}}\alpha} →\displaystyle\rightarrow ei​θ​c𝒊​α\displaystyle e^{i\theta}\,c_{{\bm{i}}\alpha}
Φ𝒊​α​β\displaystyle\Phi_{{\bm{i}}\alpha\beta} →\displaystyle\rightarrow ei​θ​Φ𝒊​α​β\displaystyle e^{i\theta}\Phi_{{\bm{i}}\alpha\beta}
ℱ1​𝒊\displaystyle\mathcal{F}_{1{\bm{i}}} →\displaystyle\rightarrow ℱ1​𝒊\displaystyle\mathcal{F}_{1{\bm{i}}}
ℬ𝒊\displaystyle\mathcal{B}_{\bm{i}} →\displaystyle\rightarrow ℬ𝒊\displaystyle\mathcal{B}_{\bm{i}}
ℱ𝒊\displaystyle\mathcal{F}_{\bm{i}} →\displaystyle\rightarrow ℱ𝒊.\displaystyle\mathcal{F}_{\bm{i}}\,. (A.5)

When we condense ⟨Φ𝒊​α​β⟩=Φ​δα​β\langle\Phi_{{\bm{i}}\alpha\beta}\rangle=\Phi\,\delta_{\alpha\beta}, then the U(1) and SU~​(2)\widetilde{\rm SU}(2) gauge symmetries are higgsed and tied to global symmetries, and the global symmetries revert back to those in Eqs. (4.9) and (4.10).

The SU~​(2)\widetilde{\rm SU}(2) transformation to the rotating reference form also changes the operator correspondences discussed in the main text. The f1f_{1} fermions are no longer just electrons cc, but related by

c𝒊​α∼Φ𝒊​α​β​f1​𝒊​β.c_{{\bm{i}}\alpha}\sim\Phi_{{\bm{i}}\alpha\beta}f_{1{\bm{i}}\beta}\,. (A.6)

Similarly, the generalization of Eq. (4.14) is

c𝒊​α∼Φ𝒊​α​β​f~𝒊​β​ where ​(f~𝒊↑−f~𝒊↓f~𝒊↓†f~𝒊↑†)∼ℬ†​ℱ𝒊.c_{{\bm{i}}\alpha}\sim\Phi_{{\bm{i}}\alpha\beta}\tilde{f}_{{\bm{i}}\beta}\mbox{~where~}\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}\tilde{f}_{{\bm{i}}\uparrow}&-\tilde{f}_{{\bm{i}}\downarrow}\\ \tilde{f}_{{\bm{i}}\downarrow}^{\dagger}&\tilde{f}_{{\bm{i}}\uparrow}^{\dagger}\end{array}\right)\sim\mathcal{B}^{\dagger}\mathcal{F}_{\bm{i}}\,. (A.7)

For the spin operator of the spin liquid, Eq. (3.32) is replaced by

S𝒊​ℓ∼−14​Tr​(Φ~𝒊†​σℓ​Φ~𝒊​σm)​Tr​(ℱ𝒊​σz​σm​T​σz​ℱ𝒊†),{S}_{{\bm{i}}\ell}\sim-\frac{1}{4}\mbox{Tr}(\tilde{\Phi}_{\bm{i}}^{\dagger}\sigma^{\ell}\tilde{\Phi}_{\bm{i}}\sigma^{m})\,\mbox{Tr}(\mathcal{F}_{{\bm{i}}}^{\phantom{\dagger}}\sigma^{z}{\sigma}^{mT}\sigma^{z}\mathcal{F}_{{\bm{i}}}^{\dagger})\,, (A.8)

where ℓ,m=x,y,z\ell,m=x,y,z, and Φ~\tilde{\Phi} is the 2×22\times 2 matrix of the complex numbers Φα​β\Phi_{\alpha\beta}. It can be checked that all three expressions in Eqs. (A.6-A.8) are invariant under all gauge transformations. In establishing Eq. (A.8), we use the following identity which lifts spinor, VV, to vector, OO, representations of SU(2)

V†V=1,V†σℓV=Oℓ​mσm⇒OTO=1.V^{\dagger}V=1,\quad V^{\dagger}\sigma^{\ell}V=O_{\ell m}\sigma^{m}\quad\Rightarrow\quad O^{T}O=1\,. (A.9)

Now we can employ the above gauge and global symmetries to obtain the complete Hamiltonian of the ALM in terms of the U𝒊​𝒋U_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}, U~𝒊​𝒋\widetilde{U}_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}, and a𝒊​𝒋a_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}} gauge fields, the bosonic Higgs fields Φ\Phi and BB, and the fermionic matter fields cc, f1f_{1}, and ff. Alternatively, the Hamiltonian can also be derived by the decoupling of the interlayer exchange interactions [4, 105], as discussed earlier in this appendix when we introduced the matter fields. The Hamiltonian of Eqs. (5.4), (2.4), (3.2.1), (5.3), and (4.17) is replaced by

ℋALM\displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{\rm ALM} =\displaystyle= ℋKLg+ℋS​L​f+ℋY+ℰ2​[B,U]+ℰ4​[B,U]\displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{\rm KLg}+\mathcal{H}_{SLf}+\mathcal{H}_{Y}+\mathcal{E}_{2}[B,U]+\mathcal{E}_{4}[B,U]
ℋKLg\displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{\rm KLg} =\displaystyle= ∑𝒊,𝒋[−t𝒊​𝒋​c𝒊​α†​c𝒋​α−t1,𝒊​𝒋​f1​𝒊​α†​ei​a𝒊​𝒋​U~i​j,α​β​f1​𝒋​β]\displaystyle\sum_{{\bm{i}},{\bm{j}}}\left[-t_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}c^{\dagger}_{{\bm{i}}\alpha}c_{{\bm{j}}\alpha}-t_{1,{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}f^{\dagger}_{1{\bm{i}}\alpha}e^{ia_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}}\widetilde{U}_{ij,\alpha\beta}f_{1{\bm{j}}\beta}\right]
−∑𝒊(c𝒊​α†Φ𝒊​α​βf1​𝒊​β+f1​𝒊​α†Φ𝒊​β​α∗c𝒊​β)\displaystyle~~~~~~-\sum_{{\bm{i}}}(c^{\dagger}_{{\bm{i}}\alpha}\Phi_{{\bm{i}}\alpha\beta}f_{1{\bm{i}}\beta}+f^{\dagger}_{1{\bm{i}}\alpha}\Phi^{\ast}_{{\bm{i}}\beta\alpha}c_{{\bm{i}}\beta})
ℋS​L​f\displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{SLf} =\displaystyle= i​J2​∑⟨𝒊​𝒋⟩e𝒊​𝒋​[Tr​(ℱ𝒊†​U𝒊​𝒋​ℱ𝒋​σz​U~𝒊​𝒋T​σz)−Tr​(ℱ𝒋†​U𝒋​𝒊​ℱ𝒊​σz​U~𝒋​𝒊T​σz)]\displaystyle\frac{iJ}{2}\sum_{\langle{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}\rangle}e_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}\left[\mbox{Tr}\left(\mathcal{F}_{{\bm{i}}}^{\dagger}U_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}^{\phantom{\dagger}}\mathcal{F}_{{\bm{j}}}^{\phantom{\dagger}}\sigma^{z}\widetilde{U}_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}^{T}\sigma^{z}\right)-\mbox{Tr}\left(\mathcal{F}_{{\bm{j}}}^{\dagger}U_{{\bm{j}}{\bm{i}}}^{\phantom{\dagger}}\mathcal{F}_{{\bm{i}}}^{\phantom{\dagger}}\sigma^{z}\widetilde{U}_{{\bm{j}}{\bm{i}}}^{T}\sigma^{z}\right)\right]
ℋY\displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{Y} =\displaystyle= ∑𝒊[i(B1​𝒊f𝒊​α†f1​𝒊​α−B2​𝒊εα​βf𝒊​αf1​𝒊​β)+H.c.\displaystyle\sum_{\bm{i}}\left[i\left(B_{1{\bm{i}}}^{\vphantom{\dagger}}f_{{\bm{i}}\alpha}^{\dagger}f_{1{\bm{i}}\alpha}^{\vphantom{\dagger}}-B_{2{\bm{i}}}^{\vphantom{\dagger}}\varepsilon_{\alpha\beta}^{\vphantom{\dagger}}f_{{\bm{i}}\alpha}^{\vphantom{\dagger}}f_{1{\bm{i}}\beta}^{\vphantom{\dagger}}\right)+\mbox{H.c.}\right. (A.10)
+ig¯(B1​𝒊f𝒊​α†Φ𝒊​β​α∗c𝒊​β−B2​𝒊εα​βf𝒊​αΦ𝒊​γ​β∗c𝒊​γ)+H.c.].\displaystyle~~~~\left.+i\bar{g}\left(B_{1{\bm{i}}}^{\vphantom{\dagger}}f_{{\bm{i}}\alpha}^{\dagger}\Phi^{\ast}_{{\bm{i}}\beta\alpha}c_{{\bm{i}}\beta}^{\vphantom{\dagger}}-B_{2{\bm{i}}}^{\vphantom{\dagger}}\varepsilon_{\alpha\beta}^{\vphantom{\dagger}}f_{{\bm{i}}\alpha}^{\vphantom{\dagger}}\Phi^{\ast}_{{\bm{i}}\gamma\beta}c_{{\bm{i}}\gamma}^{\vphantom{\dagger}}\right)+\mbox{H.c.}\right]\,.

The terms in ℰ2​[B,U]+ℰ4​[B,U]\mathcal{E}_{2}[B,U]+\mathcal{E}_{4}[B,U] remain unchanged from those in Eq. (4.17). We can also add Maxwell terms for the U(1) gauge field a𝒊​𝒋a_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}, Yang-Mills terms for the SU~​(2)\widetilde{\rm SU}(2) gauge field U~𝒊​𝒋\widetilde{U}_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}} and a Higgs potential for Φ\Phi and U~𝒊​𝒋\widetilde{U}_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}.

In the pseudogap regime studied in Sections 3-6, we condensed the Higgs field Φ𝒊​α​β=Φ​δα​β\Phi_{{\bm{i}}\alpha\beta}=\Phi\delta_{\alpha\beta}, and ignored its flucutations. The coupling constant in ℋY\mathcal{H}_{Y} in Eq. (A.10) is related to that in Eq. (5.3) by g=g¯​Φ∗g=\bar{g}\Phi^{\ast}. The constant Φ\Phi produces the hole pocket and anti-nodal pseudogap in the spectrum of cc and f1f_{1}. The constant Φ\Phi also allowed us to set the SU~​(2)\widetilde{\rm SU}(2) gauge field to U~𝒊​𝒋=1\widetilde{U}_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}=1, and the U(1) gauge field a𝒊​𝒋a_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}} to zero.

In the strange metal regime studied in Section 8, we worked in the approximation of ignoring the coupling to the bottom layer of 𝑺2{\bm{S}}_{2} spins. This can be achieved in Eq. (A.10) by setting B=0B=0. We further neglected the U(1) gauge field a𝒊​𝒋a_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}} and the SU~​(2)\widetilde{\rm SU}(2) gauge field U~𝒊​𝒋\widetilde{U}_{{\bm{i}}{\bm{j}}}, and only included the spacetime fluctuations of the diagonal component Φ\Phi coupled to the fermions cc and f1f_{1}.
